utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning everyone. Judge Chowhan is unwell this morning. He may be with us later, but we've decided to proceed on the basis of Rule 15 bis for the moment. I'm sorry we're starting late, but that was the result, apparently, of a delay in the earlier case which sat to a point where we had also to be delayed. We said we would deal with the objections to the evidence of K79. There was an objection in that case at the outset to the evidence on its entirety on the ground of relevance and lack of notice. We said that we would determine the ultimate admissibility of the evidence at the end of the examination; and over the three days that the witness was here, the Chamber received several objections to portions of the witness's evidence which it decided to rule upon at the close of that evidence. I think they came exclusively from Mr. Lukic. I'm not -- I can't remember for sure that there wasn't one from someone else, and it may be at the outset Mr. Ackerman did ultimately associate himself with the general objection to admitting the evidence at all. The Chamber is conscious of the relevance of its decision on Witness K82 in this area. In that decision issued on the 3rd of October, we held that the evidence was in fact admissible pursuant to Rules 89 and 93, but we then exercised our distress to exclude it for reasons which are set out in the decision, largely on the basis that the evidence went to alleged crimes committed in Kosovo that were not mentioned in the indictment, which the Prosecution had had in relation to that witness ample time to deal with because they had known about him for a period of years. But for the reasons that we decided that in theory at least that evidence was admissible in terms of Rule 89 and 93, we have come to the conclusion that K79's evidence is also admissible in theory. When it comes to the exercise of our discretion to decide whether to actually admit it or not, there are a number of distinguishing factors in relation to K79. The evidence he gave is relevant to inter alia the events at Suva Reka and in that area that are charged in the indictment, as well as to incidents in 1998 that are relevant to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise as alleged in paragraph 95. And the evidence is also relevant to certain other localities mentioned in the indictment. So it does appear to us that this evidence is relevant and of probative value. There are other issues, of course, to take account of in exercising discretion. For example, the length of time that the Prosecution have been aware of the evidence and the notice that they gave to the Defence, and also we have to be satisfied that in all the circumstances admitting this evidence would not cause unfair prejudice to the Defence. In contrast to K82, the evidence of K79 came to the attention of the Prosecution only shortly before the start of the trial. It was intimated as quickly as appears reasonable in all the circumstances; and although it did not lead to an amendment of the indictment or specific attention being drawn to it in the pre-trial brief, the Rule 65 ter list made clear the issues that would be dealt with by that evidence because the notice stated clearly that all matters raised in the witness's statement would be the subject of evidence in court, and that statement was disclosed because of the delayed disclosure regime on the 31st of July. So the issues upon which the witness gave evidence were adequately heralded in the indictment, the Rule 65 ter summary, and his statement. We've concluded that it would not cause unfair prejudice to the Defence to admit the evidence. In all the circumstances, therefore, we have decided to admit the evidence of K79. What weight to give that evidence, of course, is for the Trial Chamber to determine in due course, and indeed we might give it quite different weight in relation to some issues than we will in relation to others which are much more marginal and less clearly the subject of issues in the indictment. We also take this opportunity, again, to remind the Prosecution to focus the adducement of evidence on the most important issues in the case; namely, the alleged crimes in paragraph 72 and 75 of the indictment and issues going to the individual criminal responsibility of the accused. For the avoidance of doubt, I make it clear that the evidence of K79 is admitted pursuant to Rules 54, 89, and 93. It's come to our attention that a witness scheduled for next week is K54 and that similar issues may arise in relation to the evidence of that witness. It would be helpful to us, I think, if these issues were focused sooner rather than later. If there is going to be objection to that witness in his entirety or to specific segments of the evidence, then it would be helpful to have written notification of that soon so that we can address the issue rather than be faced with it on the morning and spend valuable in-court time looking at issues which we can consider outwith court. It's plain that there is a possibility of some disruption in the court schedule because of the availability of witnesses. There are two matters that we wish to draw to the attention of the Prosecution in that regard. Number one is that a witness who appears to us readily available to fill gaps would be Mr. Coo, and it may even be that his evidence could be slotted in at an appropriate stage where, otherwise, time would be lost. However, if that's going to be done, we need to be clear about how his evidence is to be presented. And since the Chamber has decided not to hear him as an expert but exclusively as a witness of fact, then it's for the Prosecution to make a submission to us about how that impacts upon the report he prepared. The report may still be a useful way of presenting evidence of fact, but it will contain passages which are clearly -- which clearly purport to be expert evidence which should not be the subject of his evidence. So that has to be resolved. We said we'd have a hearing on this, but that hearing has to be triggered, I think, by the Prosecution telling us how they see our decision as having impacted on the way they propose to present the evidence. Now, it would be helpful if that could be addressed quickly so that he is available should the situation deteriorate to the point where there's a significant gap in the schedule. The second matter is that we did indicate there were significant objections to some experts that had yet to be resolved. Now, it may be that we ought to make our position a bit clearer on that. I will review that with my colleagues in the next two days, and if more guidance can be given then it will be, but there are, I think, two or three experts in respect of whom final decisions have to be taken. Obviously, Kristan could be affected by the Chamber's view of the propriety of expert evidence on at least some of the matters to which he will be asked to speak. There's an outstanding issue in relation to the rape expert. On the other hand, there are other experts in respect of whom I doubt there is an issue. So it may be that we should identify it. Are you clear on the point, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.text: We have three there. 1967, 8, and 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. 67 and 68 have previously been admitted by this Court. We're also seeking admission of P01969 under the same basis of the reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to deal with that when you come to that stage of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually that will be presented from the bar table, but I will certainly handle that when it comes up in the evidence. P00682, as referenced in paragraph 74. And that completes the documents that are listed within his statement and at this time we would tender it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Experience has taught us now that we will or should reserve any decision about admitting statements of that nature until we've heard the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should remind us at the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would also note that any of the exhibits that came from the Ministry of Defence, specifically the situation reports, those would have to be tendered under seal, as well as the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At the request of the Rule 70 provider due to confidentiality concerns. They have been redact you, had but they are still requesting that the admission be under seal as was done in the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're suggesting this statement should be held under seal. Is there a reason, a good reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the provider simply states that due to confidentiality reasons, they would request that it be tendered under seal based on the material that is found within it. This is the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an example of what might justify that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: This -- this witness, while is certainly giving testimony live, was in a unique position to see a number of -- excuse me, giving testimony in open session, was in a unique position to see and be a part of conversations taking place in Kosovo. This is it the procedure that was filed -- followed with regards to Exhibit 92 in the Limaj case, and they're just seeking the same consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time is moving on constantly. These events in some instances are more than eight years ago now. There's no suggestion that methods are being compromised by divulging the material. At the moment, it's very difficult to see why Rule 70's being applied to this, and we would urge you to take that matter up with the provider and endeavour to resolve the issue of making this an open, public evidence, including the reports. Unless there is some identifiable prejudice, after this length of time, one would have thought that this could be public.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll certainly take that up with the provider, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no option but to hold it under seal, I assume, because you tell us that there is a Rule 70 requirement. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this will be of assistance or not. In the Limaj case, there is almost a virtual waver, I would suggest. What they did in the Limaj case, because they were under seal, the Prosecutor Mr. Cayley just read them into the record in open court so that the content of them is all sitting in the transcript, even though the document itself is under seal which seems silly to think, and I agree with the Court that time has passed over. That makes no sense any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nevertheless, there are wider issues associated with the application of Rule 70, which makes it inappropriate for us to run roughshod over a requirement like this. We are -- we are bound to adhere to that requirement at the moment. All we can do is express the view that the Prosecution should take the matter up with the provider with a view to having this out in the open. It, on the face of it, does more harm than good to keep unnecessary secrets and that's a general proposition. Whether it applies in this case, is for the provider obviously to judge, but hopefully you'll persuade the provider to allow publication of anything that the provider can't offer a good reason for retaining in secret after this lapse of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll certainly make that application to the provider, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now direct the witness beginning at paragraph 7 where's discussing the forces of Serbia. In it you're giving many descriptions of the MUP as well as their special units and the VJ. Can you -- and you make some assessments with regard to the professional demeanour and the training of these individuals. Can you please describe for the Court what is it that you saw there on the ground in Kosovo which gave you the ability to differentiate between the training and the demeanour of these individual units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my time in Kosovo, which was nearly three years, I saw the build-up of this incident in Kosovo and obviously monitored very carefully the deployment of Serbian security forces throughout the length and breadth of Kosovo. It became very clear to me that there were certain units being deployed within the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the police, and also within the standing 52 Pristina Corps, which was already stationed at Vojska Jugoslavije within Kosovo itself. As regards the MUP, there were the normal what one might call policemen dressed in their normal milicija dress, and then it became evident there were other elements that were being used in different and discreet ways to achieve or attempt to achieve a military situation or solution within Kosovo itself. Initially, the Serbian security forces made it very easy by these units identifying themselves by various patches, as I described in paragraph 7 the PJP and also the ancillary equipment that these men and formations carried. Hence, it was relatively easy in the early stages to identify very clearly the various elements concerned and to put unit nominations to them. I would respectfully remind the Court that having been working in BRIXMIS, where we monitored the then Soviet forces in East Germany, this was part of my background and, therefore, one was fairly capable, I would suggest, of identifying which forces we were dealing with and at which level these forces were -- were used throughout the operations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you determine some sort of hierarchy or specialities of these individual units; and if so, can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general terms initially there were the -- the ordinary what I would call the village MUP who were carrying out duties as normal policemen do throughout the world, and these personnel soon found themselves in a very difficult situation. In order to continue operations as the situation deteriorated, the MUP then brought in what I would call the light infantry, which is the PJP, who were better armed and equipped and better trained to both hold ground and to take ground as required in a more aggressive stance as the situation, as I said, deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object to evidence being led as to training, without any foundation of how this witness knows of any specific training of any MUP units for that matter, not just the PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Crosland, on how you -- can you help us, Mr. Crosland, on how you could conclude that the PJP were better trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in -- as I've attempted to make clear to the Court, there were operations of different natures which started at a very low level and then soon rapidly increased; and in order to carry out these more complicated military operations, it was quite clear that the normal MUP were not being involved. And we very quickly found out, as I said because these people were wearing PJP and Cyrillic on their uniforms, these were the people initially dealing with the situation. There were then other more specialised units like the SAJ and the JSO who were used, as I have said, for the direct assault onto various objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is the PJP were better able to act in a more aggressive way than the MUP. Is that -- is that what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And also we saw these personnel actually carrying out operations dressed as PJP, and I believe there is photographic evidence of that in -- in one of the many reports that I made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To follow up on Judge Bonomy's inquiry in regards to the PJP being better able to act in a more aggressive way, can you please describe what it was about them, either in stature or armaments, that made them more available for these aggressive-type movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. The normal MUP regularly carried side arms and occasionally long arms, and carries out normal what I would call policing duties. When the situation deteriorated then we saw that instead of the MUP, the PJP were brought in in various formations to deal with, as I've described, more complex military manoeuvres. And the PJP, as I have described, would be what I would call the light infantry and then allowing the more specialised units to concentrate on the objectives in hand which would be dealt with by the SAJ and the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did you witness the SAJ and the JSO doing within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have reported within this, I met them on several occasions, primarily when they were about to assault one of the KLA headquarters in Malisevo. And at other times, we saw them on protection duties, particularly around the Drenica and the Jablanica areas, and also holding positions all the way down the western road from Pec in the north through Decani down to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you describe in layman's terms what you mean by the SAJ and the JSO were able to concentrate on the objectives in hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the PJP would have -- would secure the area and initiate the initial contact, and then the specialist forces would move in to assault whatever objectives they were planning to assault. As I indicated, I met a combined force at Lapusnik and Kijevo on the main Pec-Pristina road prior to their assault onto Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You use the term, in regards to the PJP, that they would "initiate the initial contact." What type of contact are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This varied considerably from a surrounding an area and possibly intimidating the inhabitants to move out, to artillery firing shells into the area as a warning to move out prior to a more major operation, cleaning operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is a reference in the statement to the attack that's been mentioned on Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I would point out at paragraph 37, which it indicates there was an operation within the Malisevo area which resulted in 30.000 missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, in paragraph 38 specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've -- you were asked a question there about how the PJP would initially make the initial contact, and you went on to say "that varied considerably from surrounding an area, possibly intimidating the inhabitants to move out, to artillery firing shells into the area as warning." Are you suggesting the PJP were using artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not, Your Honour. This was a combined MUP and VJ operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Ms. Carter, something you could perhaps help me with. We've just had evidence from a member of the PJP, as you know. My recollection, but perhaps you can correct me, was that essentially he carried the same weapons as an ordinary policeman and wore the same uniform up until March 1999. Now, is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can recall firsthand the evidence of K86, who indicated that at different times there were up to three uniforms that were used. And in regards to the PJP versus the MUP, there were separate uniforms; however, the PJP members possessed both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With that witness, I believe the one you're referring to was the parade uniform, which I doubt was being used in the field, and I think that's what the witness also testified to. The witness we had other week, just last week I believe testified they had the same weapons and same uniforms as Your Honour indicated. That's what my notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They had supplementary weapons; but when it came to the arms they are carrying, at least the arms he was carrying --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The personal weapons. Correct, that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As we've now moved on to the armaments available to the individual units, can you please describe for the Court what the individual MUP units had in their possession, as well as what the VJ had in its possession on average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. In -- within paragraphs 7, 8, and 9, I've laid out as clearly as I can the differences between the various units concerned. The Vojska Jugoslavije had obviously small arms and long arms and then had the normal assignment of heavy -- heavier weapons from T-55s [Realtime transcript read in error "P-55s"] or T-84s at times, the tanks, as well as armoured personnel carriers and M-80s, and the BOV-3s as well. What became obvious, as I mentioned in one of the paragraphs, was that some of these equipments were transferred by painting them from green, which are the VJ's colour, to blue and being used by the MUP and its entirety on various operations. The more specialised units like the SAJ and the JSO had much more up-to-date weapons, as I've indicated, the Heckler Koch, smaller weapons, as well as much more distinctive vehicles, to wit, land cruisers. And their uniforms were of a much more modern appearance. I also respectfully remind the Court that as a soldier of some 37 years, you do have an inkling for seeing people and how they behave and their demeanour as to what state of training they've had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated a number of items such as tanks by the name of -- in the record, it indicates P-55. Are you indicated P as in Paul or T as in. Tom 55?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a T-55.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And for those of us who are not familiar with heavy armaments, can you please describe for the Court what is the use and the nature of the individual items that you have described, such as the T-55, the T-84, the M-80, and the BOV-3s? Including their range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the ground in Kosovo is not particularly suitable for counter-insurgency operations from an insurgent's points of view because it's rolling open countryside in the majority of areas. There are wooded and hilly areas which provide a much better arena to -- to stage a counter-insurgency operation. The -- therefore, the ranges of the T-55 and the T-84, M-84, the tanks, I would suggest are hardly the weapons to use in a counter-insurgency operation, because they obviously do an immense amount of damage and can terrify the population fairly easily by their immense firepower and bulk. The other equipment, the armoured personnel carriers, the M-80s and BOV-3s, the BOV-3 is a tripled-barrelled anti-aircraft weapon of various calibres between 20, 30, and 40-millimetre. As I have made quite clear in this report, on many occasions, I witnessed the use of this -- these anti-aircraft weapons in destroying houses and assaulting villages. I think I'm right in saying that within the Geneva Convention, it is not allowed to use these weapons in that -- in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me for trying to clarify something, and it's possibly my lack of understanding of this, but you say the ground in Kosovo is not particularly suitable for counter-insurgency operations from and insurgent's points of view, because it's open countryside. What you do mean by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I mean by that, Your Honour, is that the insurgents if they -- if they chose to stand and fight against either the Vojska Jugoslavije or the MUP were very soon outranged by superior weaponry and then left in a difficult situation to try and withdraw to fight another day, and this was -- happened at the -- one of the first instance in Likoshani, Donji Prekaz when the Jashari family with taken down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is it's good for counter-insurgency and bad for the insurgents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. I followed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that there's quite a bit of damage that can be accomplished by the use of the T-55 and the T-84. What type of range, accuracy, and destruction are available by these tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not an armour expert. I'm an infantry and special forces soldier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just old on, please. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I believe that this witness is a fact witness, not an expert witness. And I believe that this question is not appropriate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think he's going to tell us the extent to which he is qualified to answer it. But with 37 years in the army, there's just a chance that he might know the damage that would be caused by certain tanks from a general experience point of view without having to be specifically set up as an expert. So let's hear the basis on which he's going to answer the question and then judge the answer according to the basis that he gives us, the foundation he gives us for his answer. Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I was about to say, I'm not a tank officer, an armoured officer. I'm an infantry and a special forces officer. However, I've had considerable experience in -- in dealing with unconventional warfare throughout the world and the various damages that can be inflicted by weapon systems. Both the T-55 and the M-84 will be accurate up to a range of about one and a half miles or 3.000 metres. They will deliver a shell 120 millimetre, which is about six or seven inches across, which will quite comfortably destroy a house on impact. Throughout my report I described, on the many times that I was down there with some 70 reports plus other conversations that I had direct back to London and other places, the immense destruction that was carried out by the Serbian security forces throughout the province of Kosovo. Not all of this was done by tank fire. The village of Prilep, for instance, was reduced to about three to four inches height throughout, and that was done by bulldozers and various other bits and pieces. I think the point I'm making or attempting to make is that disproportionate force was used throughout this campaign. The BOV-3, the anti-aircraft weapon with its triple barrelled and many calibres, is also a very fearsome weapon when used against primarily civilian targets. And, again, there was ample evidence of empty shell cases again scattered throughout the entire province of Kosovo during the 18 months that I was there. I hope that clears up the issue for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Crosland. You also have indicated within your statement that you saw the presence of paramilitaries within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I would just bring -- or offer from the bar table Exhibit number P927, the collegium minutes of 29 June, 1998. They were received pursuant the same type of RFA's that the other collegium minutes that were entered by this Court on January 22nd of 2007. We would hold out to the Court that they maintain the same indicia of reliability, and we would offer them from the bar table now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can that be brought up on the screen for us or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask the Court to bring up P927, specifically at page 5, referencing the third full paragraph as it relates to this witness's statement with regards to the paramilitaries at paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you identify the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're looking to page 5, third full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The paragraph beginning after the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the paragraph beginning the check-points, if you look to that paragraph and the last three lines. I'm offering this at this time, Your Honour, as it indicates both the indicia of reliability within the witness's statement in regards to what he saw paramilitaries engaged in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Collegium minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the VJ collegium, is it?.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, where the VJ is indicating that Arkan's Tigers, which were viewed reviewed by this witness, were present in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's -- with all respect, that's not what that indicates at all. You have to read it in context. If you go back to page 4, General Perisic is offering to report what data NATO is reporting regarding units, and they ask him to go ahead and tell him what NATO is reporting and then he tells him that NATO is reporting the presence of these paramilitary formations. I believe that's the context in which this is. I don't think he's telling him what units are there. He's telling him what NATO is saying are there, if you read starting at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Go back to page 4 then to look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's got, "General, sir, if you consider it necessary, I can report on what data NATO has on the army on the 52nd Corps," and then goes on to report,"I believe what NATO is saying is going on..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman's suggesting that what we're getting here is a report from Major-General Milovanovic of what NATO were -- or at least what the view of NATO was of the factual position.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It is a reference into what NATO was reporting, but what you will not find is a correction indicating that these forces were in fact not engaged in Kosovo and that NATO is reporting wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a stretch, if I've ever heard one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for debate later. What -- where we are at the moment is that we have minutes of the VJ collegium. It's not being suggested that they are not the minutes of the VJ collegium or they are in some way inaccurate, and the Prosecution offer them for later interpretation, as I understand the position. And on that basis, these will be admitted. We have a context here to assess their relevance, and we will admit them for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I try and help the Court on this basis in that intelligence reports from NATO were based on the NATO defence attaches like myself who reported direct back to their individual Ministry of Defence or Department of Defence, and therefore the statement has got that authority. I personally had other signal intelligence that indicated quite clearly that elements of the paramilitaries were based in Zvecin [phoen] just north of Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a new objection then, because it hardly can be offered as evidence that corroborates the witness when it's based on the witness's reports. I think that's quite a circular argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's again a matter of weight, Mr. Ivetic. In due course you will be able to make the point that he may be a source -- in fact, for all we know, Colonel Crosland is the particular source of this report, and you'll be able to make that submission when you invite us to evaluate the evidence. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, where did you see paramilitaries within Kosovo, and can you please describe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said stated in paragraph 15, it was quite clear that there were other forces outside both the MUP and the VJ operating within the whole of Kosovo, and as I've made clear here by the licence plates they had come from all over the place, including Skopje and Macedonia and Novi Sad and Belgrade. And these personnel, as I've described, were fit, were young, and were extremely confident of their ability to influence the situation in many ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on your years of experience within the military as well as your years and experience with insurgency forces throughout the world, why would you bring in a paramilitary unit such as these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's been made clear in the NATO report that these personnel had had experience in Bosnia. And, therefore, as part of the overall armory of the Serbian security forces, if you wish to call it that, these personnel would be used in operations as they had been done -- had been used throughout the Bosnia war.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were these paramilitary units out in the open so that the -- it appeared that the MUP and VJ would be aware of their presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- they were relatively secret about the way that they moved about. When they did come out, I think it was a deliberate policy of influencing the civilian population that if they didn't comply with what was going on, then there would be trouble, as has been proved on many occasions within the Bosnia war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In which paragraph was the reference to Prilep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One minute, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is 1046. I don't know if right now would be a good time for the break, but in the break I could locate the paragraph reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to clarify this, if we can, before we break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have indication of paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 41, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you talk about seeing Prilep razed to the ground, that was during that visit referred to in paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not quite correct, Your Honour. We were -- we were taken on this particular occasion towards a place called Glodjane, where the Serbian forces said there had been a massacre of some six to eight persons. I think the point of this paragraph, if I may say so, is that we were being driven there by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when was it you've -- you saw the state that Prilep was left in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the whole of the summer, Prilep came under bombardment on a name of occasions. It was on a junction that was close to an MUP vehicle check-point; in other words, a stationary position. And I would readily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 42, in fact, you deal with a specific point that you made in your evidence just now, and I just wondered when it was you saw it in that condition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like that condition so throughout most of the summer of 1998. And I think in one of my reports, it may not be attested here, there were photographs showing the -- the amount of damage concerned. And paragraph 43 refers to more damage in Decani, Pec, and Djakovica, the Albanian areas in particular being burnt out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to break at this stage, and the usher will show you where to wait. During the break, we'll go into closed session while you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 29 of your statement where you were further discussions of paramilitaries, and I believe it's indicating the concept of the paramilitaries starting something for the other forces to then follow up on. Can you please develop that a bit further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This paragraph 29, Your Honours, we had indication that there were paramilitaries. We were based in Pec at the time and we saw fairly large convoys of -- of 4-by-4 vehicles associated with the paramilitaries; and we then followed them back over the border into Baranja or Ivangrad in Montenegro, Crna Gora, and that is where we found quite a few cars. I can't remember exactly how many of them from this distance. And it was quite clear that they were being corralled in Montenegro prior to being deployed into Kosovo, and we then came across them in various places throughout the time I spent in Kosovo, which indicated that they were part and parcel of the -- the Serbian security force armory to contain this situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you indicate in that paragraph that their --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate in your statement that their job was to stir up trouble so that the MUP would step in and sort out the participants. Can you give some examples of this stirring up of trouble and what happened on behalf of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated in paragraph 29, there was an incident which we specifically detailed in Pristina in 1998 where six to eight persons beat up an ITN journalist. There were other instances of this around -- around the area, and it was generally known that they were being used as a unit to impress upon the civilian population that they should heed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does that phrase mean, "to impress upon the civilian population they should heed what was going on?" That doesn't mean anything to me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. What I'm -- what I mean is that, as I say, it was all part of the Serbian security force armory to get across to the Kosovo Albanians that if they didn't behave or if they supported the KLA, they would be the object of attention by both the paramilitaries and the rest of the Serbian security forces. It was all a question of -- of a tactic of fear to instil in the local population which is primarily Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that the Serbian forces were trying to get across a point to those who supported the KLA or were in the KLA. Is that an exclusive list of who the ire of the Serb forces was directed upon, or did the general civilian population fall into that group as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd been visiting Kosovo since probably the first trip in September 1996 and, therefore, had seen that contrary to what had been reported before that the majority of population was Kosovo Albanian. Therefore, the main -- in a lot of areas, it was Kosovo Albanian entirely. And really, the goldfish in the bowl, if I can use that expression, was actually the -- the remnant Serb population, and I will put it at approximately 2 million Albanians to about 400.000 Serbs. And this population, prior to 1998, had lived in relative harmony throughout the entire area. When the Kosovo Liberation Army appeared late -- I suppose the first [Realtime transcript read in error "International Red Cross"] instance was 1997 and then the more serious instance started in 1998, the Serbian security forces de facto realised that the majority of the population being Kosovo Albanian could possibly support, and I stress could, the KLA or the Kosovo Liberation Army. Now, many of the Kosovo Albanians, in my opinion, really didn't want either the Serbian security forces there or the KLA. Kosovo was a potentially and is today a fertile and rich area, and most of them had come from Albania, which was left in a dreadful state by Enver Hodzic and other people. And they saw Kosovo as a place to go to make their money and do their business which the Kosovo Albanians are actually capable of doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somehow in page 40, line 11, the words "International Red Cross" have crept in there, and he didn't say anything about the International Red Cross. And I'd also suggest that the answer was really not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it was a reference to the initial instance was 1997 and the most serious instance started in 1998. You may take note of what Mr. Ackerman said because although information was provided, this sort of conclusion that the question was seeking was not at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your answer, you indicate that most of the people within Kosovo just wanted to be left alone. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have maintained that the hard-core element of the Kosovo Liberation Army was in the low hundreds, about 400, throughout most of the campaign. This increased obviously towards the end of the campaign when it became clear that NATO was intervening and the pressure was on the Serbian security forces. What I would say is that the -- the rest of the Kosovo Albanian population, as I have indicated, wished to -- to be perfectly friendly, perfectly fair, and in the majority of cases got on with their Serbian neighbours with whom they had lived for in many cases for hundreds of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So when you were making reference to the paramilitaries starting trouble and then the MUP sorting it out, did these people who did not have any desire or any support of the KLA, did they face the same ire of the MUP or were they spared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you have touched, if I may say so, on the key, the key point that everyone recognised the -- the Serbian security forces and the former Republic of Yugoslavia, as it then was, was facing a counter-terrorist movement in the shape of the Kosovo Liberation Army. What did not help the situation was the way that the Serbian security forces in their entirety, from paramilitary through the MUP and the Vojska Jugoslavije, reacted with total over -- overforce and aggression in destroying villages, businesses, and the -- the whole way of life of most of the -- the Kosovo Albanians within the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying that the Serb security force as it then was "was facing a counter-terrorist movement in the shape of the Kosovo Liberation Army?" That's not what I would understand by counter-terrorism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were facing an insurgency, Your Honour, in the shape of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is counter-terrorism not what you do to fight terrorism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do you really mean to say a terrorist movement in the shape of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were facing a terrorist movement in the shape of the Kosovo Liberation Army or, if you may wish, an insurgency movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I understand the sensitivities of using the expression terrorist, but I just want to be clear what your answer amounts to. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, just to clarify, because you've given a number of statements over the years to the Office of the Prosecution, in your assessment was the Kosovo Liberation Army a terrorist movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have stated quite clearly, the Kosovo Liberation Army was a terrorist organisation. It began as a fledgling organisation in the late 19 -- probably late 1997, it first came to our -- our notice, and then the -- the fledgling organisation gradually developed throughout 1998 to when in -- in the late autumn of 1998, it was a fairly well-organised and supplied organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you're discussing the counter-terrorism problem that you believe the Serbian side was facing, was it narrowed to the 400 people that you would actually consider KLA members, or did the civilian population also pay a price?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sadly, with -- despite many conversations with both General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic and latterly with senior personnel within the Pristina Corps, the actions of the Serbian security forces, which were extremely heavy handed in a lot of cases, eventually managed, I would suggest, to drive a lot of the Kosovo Albanians against the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And to round out what made up the entirety of the Serbian security forces, in paragraph 19, you begin making some reference to Serb villages and their village defence forces. Can you flesh that out a bit more? What are we dealing with when you're referring to these civilian defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think throughout Kosovo I probably came across about eight or nine villages that had local Serbian defence forces. I would suggest they are, in the region of local home defence, a bit like dad's army in English during World War II. But within the whole scope of having in excess of 13.000 Vojska Jugoslavije already stationed within Pristina -- or within Kosovo, sorry, and up to 10.000 MUP, the added firepower, if you will, of these very small contingents was pretty insignificant. But their job was to defend their -- their isolated settlements in many cases, and one can understand entirely why they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally encounter these village defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I said, I visited, I think, about eight villages; Obilic being one and Kijevo on the main Pec-Pristina road being a particular flashpoint area because it was surrounded by Kosovo Albanian villages and, therefore, the object of quite a good measure of treatment from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you have encountered these village defence forces, have they ever served any aggression upon you, such as not allowing access or any other more caustic measure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that as a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I can rephrase if the Court would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your times with these village defence forces, were you treated amicably or were there times where there was a level aggressiveness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that remains leading. If she wants to ask the question in a non-leading way, how -- how did he encounter these people, what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, how did they treat you, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they treated us very reasonably. I speak Serbian, and we were treated as friendly people. If -- the only people who really tried to stop us were actually the KLA who wouldn't actually accept the licna karta, our diplomatic identity card, because this was now the province of Kosovo Albania run by the KLA, which I'm afraid I did not agree with at all. And these villages were, as I said, very isolated, some of them quite poor; and therefore in a humanitarian way, one was trying to maintain a firm and fair view of what was going on throughout the entire province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to pull up now paragraph -- I'm sorry, P number 687.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just was brought to my attention as these items are to go under seal, at least as we are today, we would ask the -- they not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Does that mean hard copies need to be provided to the witness, or can he see it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within this situation report, not only do you indicate the vehicles that you viewed being painted from green to blue, you also indicate that the VJ exercises are used to cover observation tasks. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Carter, where exactly are you speaking from?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It should be, I believe, page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't -- I haven't got that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have it now, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do so, I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the bottom, you indicated that you believe the VJ is giving materiel support, and you go on from there. Can you please expand upon that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had cover the positions about various vehicles being repainted and reallocated, which were not within the original order of battle of the -- of the MUP, and this concerned the M-80 APCs, the BOV-3 anti-aircraft vehicles as, I indicated earlier in my statement. As regards the tasks of the Vojska Jugoslavije, when I joined as defence attache in 1996, we were briefed by the Foreign Liaison Service of the role of the Vojska Jugoslavije in the then-Federal Republic of -- former Republic of Yugoslavia. And, in essence, that was an international border security task which roamed from about 500 metres to two kilometres, depending on the situation. It became clear, as the insurgency grew in 1998, that the Vojska Jugoslavije had additional tasks, and this was made clear by General Ojdanic in August, I think, at a briefing to the Belgrade Attache Association that four extra tasks had been given to the Vojska Jugoslavije, again, in support of the MUP that had had primacy in dealing with an internal situation as was ongoing within the province of Kosovo. The additional task for the Vojska Jugoslavije were the -- that they should guard the lines of communication through -- through Kosovo, various deployment areas that were historically areas they had deployed to and exercise areas, as well as the security border scenario that by then had reached probably ten in some cases 15 kilometres in width. So this meant that there had been a fundamental change in the constitutional deployment of the Vojska Jugoslavije, which the defence council had initiated, as I said, because the worsening situation within Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate that there was expansion of the -- the use of the VJ. Did you have discussions with General Ojdanic with regards to this expansion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in that it was quite clear that despite constant reference to General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, who I met on a fairly regular basis, that I had firsthand evidence and photographic evidence of the VJ being involved in joint MUP and Vojska Jugoslavije operations. General Ojdanic, as Chief of the General Staff -- or, sorry, Colonel of the General Staff at that time and then chief the General Staff afterwards, chose to ignore this. And it was not until his briefing to the Belgrade Attache Association, which I think is referred to in this report on the 28th or 27th of August, that I then handed him video evidence that I had seen and witnessed at firsthand over four hours of shelling by multi-rocket launchers, artillery, and tank fire in direct support of combined joint MUP and VJ operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If Ojdanic is acknowledging it in August, had there been an open communication about it throughout all the other times that you had seen the VJ and MUP acting in accordance with one another throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is leading again, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back slightly here. Your discussions with Ojdanic were when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the -- the month of August, Your Honour, when he was asked to give an update to the Belgrade Attache Association, of which I was the president, because of the general concern that the situation in Kosovo was serious, as I've indicated already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can come do that. I'm just interested in the time, and is that what you're referring to in paragraph 42?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You talk about a video. Do we still have the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, because this was -- was given across to the foreign liaison service in Beograd, and I don't have any idea whether it's still in evidence or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You didn't make a copy at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure there was a copy. I know there was a copy sent to my Ministry of Defence and other allied Ministry of Defence. Where that copy is now, I -- I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next question to which objection was taken was whether there had been any earlier communication or indeed later in 1998, communication with General Ojdanic about similar matters. What's the position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- Your Honour, there was ongoing communication with the foreign liaison service, which was the -- the entree to the Vojska Jugoslavije General Staff, through either personal interviews with General Dimitrijevic or General Perisic. Now, I would presume that that was passed on to -- to General Ojdanic, as then as the -- the Chief of Staff, and he was then summoned -- I beg your pardon, sir. He was then summoned to give a briefing to the Attache Association to try and allay the alarm that was being raised by the excessive use of force of all the Serbian forces within -- within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the only occasion you met General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I met him about three times, sir, yes, partly as my duties as president of the Belgrade Attache Association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On what occasions did you meet with General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the occasion is here stated, ma'am, on the 28th of August was really, as I've said to the Court, was really to confirm that we were not prepared, having got firsthand evidence and witnessed it myself, that there were combined operations between the VJ and the MUP and that excessive force was being used in what was meant to be a counter-insurgency operation. And I would suggest that to use tanks, heavy armoured vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- defence weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The question was on what occasion did you meet with General Ojdanic. So far, he said August 28, and I think we're waiting for the other allegedly two occasions. All this other stuff is advocacy, not testimony, Your Honour, as Your Honours well know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer so far has been dealing with the 28th of August, if you see the beginning of it, Mr. Sepenuk. If you can tell us roughly the other occasions, Mr. Crosland, then Ms. Carter can ask further questions about these if she wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The specific dates, Your Honour -- I mean, we're talking nearly ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said to the Court, in my duty as the Belgrade Attache Association, one would meet socially with General Ojdanic at various receptions and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is the simple answer that these other occasions didn't involve notifying him of the excessive use of force by a combination of the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. This occasion was used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the one that matters, from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my point of view and from the point of view of the other NATO attaches is this is where we were making the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in your -- in your written statement, you say that major or key people like General Ojdanic did not seem to want to hear this information, and -- and that could cover a number of things referred to there, which I think can be divided into two main subjects. One is the extent of the devastation, and the other is the combined nature of the operations. Now, what was it they didn't want to hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, both. Bearing in mind that I'd also escorted around through the area during the -- the summer of 1998 the G8, five or six ambassadors with Ambassador Donnelly, my ambassador. So not only was it a military viewpoint but also a political viewpoint that had been seen by a considerable number of people. And I will make the point, if I may, that having travelled in Kosovo since 1996, one had seen it in its peaceful condition and then to see it during 1998 gradually being rumbled was pretty devastating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the distinction is important here. I can understand the point you're making that -- that you were trying to alert senior personnel to the degree of damage being done; but on the other matter, the combined nature of the operations, are you saying that there was an element of denial about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was considerable denial right up until the 27th, 28th of August when we presented this video and my own statement that I had witnessed fire; and, again, when Lord Ashdown was with us in August, he and the BBC had also seen ongoing firing within the Suva Reka area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I got the impression from earlier answers you gave here that on the 28th of August there was some change, but that's not reflected in your statement, I don't think. So what is the situation once the video has been handed over and viewed? You then have a meeting of the defence attache's association at which General Ojdanic is present. Is that the correct order of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. General -- Your Honour, General Ojdanic was asked, presumably from pressure within the Vojska Jugoslavije and ourselves, to brief the Belgrade Attache Association on the situation within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that after he had viewed your video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, he had viewed it. I couldn't be certain, but he -- in that briefing, he continued to deny that there had been any combined operations until I specifically said that I had seen four hours of shelling and so on, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was his reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as I've said in the report, sir, that he was fairly phlegmatic about it and that force would be met with force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I recollect such a reference, but where is that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 and 51, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, paragraph 50 and 51.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yep -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there you say that General Ojdanic had accepted your observations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had accepted them in so much as he couldn't refute them. Whether he -- he wished to actually acknowledge them, I would suggest by his answer that it was not -- it was a negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Just to be clear on the time line, prior to you handing the video over to Ojdanic and saying, "Look, this is a joint operation," what was the party line in regards to whether the MUP and VJ were acting separately or together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The party line on the whole was that there was -- there was no collusion between the VJ and the MUP. We have the -- the start here of a break within the Vojska Jugoslavije where General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, as I indicated, that they were outside the chain of command that was going direct from President Milosevic down to General Pavkovic; and that General Pavkovic could see that this was an opportunity for him to produce a result for his -- for President Milosevic and, therefore, the chain of command was starting to fragment within the Vojska Jugoslavije.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So the party line maintains that MUP and VJ are separate, with the exception of the two gentlemen, Perisic and Dimitrijevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. At the point you then hand the video to Ojdanic and put it to his face, is that when the party line changes and there's acknowledgement on behalf of the VJ as a whole that there are joint operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was -- no, I don't think there was. There was a -- a resignation that they had been given factual evidence that was correct and difficult to refute, but they didn't wish to acknowledge that evidence per se.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when Ojdanic replies, "force will be met with force," what type of force was the KLA inflicting upon the VJ after you saw -- or during the time of this four hours of direct and indirect firing upon this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The KLA had no answer to the heavier weapons that both the tanks, the multi-rocket launcher systems, and the artillery that was deployed against various positions primarily in the area of Junik and from a firing position at Blace over to Suva Reka and other villages that came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The KLA did not have any weapons that could match these at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And to go back to your previous testimony, we're dealing 400 KLA versus how many combined MUP and VJ are at issue in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've stated here, ma'am, the estimate was about 12 to 13.000 Vojska Jugoslavije, which were stationed within Kosovo within the Pristina Corps and at major times between 8 to 10.000 MUP that were brought in to -- to the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could look for a moment again at paragraph 51 - maybe I haven't noted the changes you were making to that properly - you say that on the 26th and 27th of September, you and Ashdown showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of VJ shelling in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was, with respect, was pointed out as being incorrect when we started the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what that was changed to on approximately the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Lord Ashdown did not show Ojdanic photographic evidence. He went to see President Milosevic, I think on the 28th of September. That has been, in my opinion, the two dates, 26th, 27th of September and August have been muddled up in the -- when this brief was put together; and that, as I say, was pointed out by -- by Ms. Carter at the beginning of this session, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not how I noted it. It must be my mistake. I know the sentence was moved to the beginning of paragraph 50. Did you also change these dates at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. Number 51 should have read,"On approximately 28 September 1998, Lord Ashdown also went to see Milosevic." So 51 is in relation to Lord Ashdown and a September date. Everything with relation to August, it should be in paragraph 50 in relation to the conversation between this witness and Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that. That's the last part of paragraph 51. I've got that. But what change did you make to the first sentence of paragraph 51, when you moved it to the beginning of paragraph 50?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I moved it up and changed, "On 26 to 27 August, 1998, I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the shelling of Suva Reka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So September gets changed to August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think you have that right, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Carter has that right at all. If she's reading from the supplemental information sheet, the supplemental information sheet says, Your Honour, that paragraph 50, the first sentence should read, "On 26, 27 September 1998, I showed Ojdanic..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I've noted you doing this morning in the changes you made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I apologise, Your Honour. I'm looking off of my notes to the statement itself. It is a failing on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's get back to the witness then. There's no point in relaying this through you. Let's get it clear. Could you have in front of you, please, paragraph 51 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we were invited to remove the first two sentences from there and put them at the beginning of paragraph 50. Now, tell me, are there any other changes to be made to these two sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand it, paragraph 51, from my position, should read,"On the 28th of September, Lord Ashdown had a meeting with Milosevic directly after his visit to Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But that's the last -- you'll see that's there in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, in fact, it should be on approximately the 28th of September, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He went to see Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And made comments to Milosevic you believe about the shelling. But look at the beginning of that where you're talking about what you showed -- ignore Ashdown, because I think we were told to delete the reference to him. But there was a date at the beginning of 51, and then it said, "I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka on the 27th of August. His reaction was that force would be met with appropriate force." Now, what date did you show him that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was either on the -- that was either on the 27th or the 28th of August, Your Honour, which is when he gave the briefing to the Belgrade Attache Association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. This is very confusing in the extreme, Your Honour, because I have in front of me the supplemental information sheet. And it's specifically stated here, Your Honours, that paragraph 50, the first sentence should now read, and I quote: "On 26, 27 September 1998, I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka on 27 August 1998." That's the way it reads, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've now got the organ grinder here and we can ask him directly, and he's told us that his recollection is it was the 27th or 28th of August and that that is separate from the period to which the contact between Ashdown and Milosevic relates. Can I be clear about one other thing. On the 27th of August, when you observed events at Suva Reka, was Ashdown there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He was there with the BBC crew and Ambassador Donnelly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he made a second visit in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He made a second visit, Your Honour. Exactly when, I can't be sure without looking at specific information, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you will see, in fact, that the last sentence of 51 talks about seeing Milosevic after his first visit. So we have a rather messy couple of paragraphs here which I think if you really want to rely on this as significant evidence, you better start between and go through this and find out what the witness's best recollection of the events covered by these two paragraphs is and delete the paragraphs from your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] as of now on paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would actually seek an amendment as opposed to redaction of those two paragraphs because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We're not getting into the situation we got into with an earlier witness where we start cutting and pasting. This is a result of the technological age that isn't in keeping with presenting evidence in its most reliable form to the Court, no matter how it might suit technology today. So let's hear what the witness has to say about these events from his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when was the shelling of Suva Reka in which you watched four hours of direct and indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, ma'am, the report was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe she's asked for his recollection. I believe he's reading from a report now. I'm not sure that's proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a statement he has already made. No doubt you'll be confronting him with it if he departs substantially from it in any event. I think it's unrealistic, I think, in the environment where you're not dealing with a jury to take away the document that -- that was the basis on which this confusion arose. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we'll allow the witness to do his best with all the material available to him to give us his recollection of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the witness is to have all material available, there actually is a situation report at P02553 in which the meeting with the defence attaches by Ojdanic is referenced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now presenting this as oral evidence live from the witness, so you decide how you want to lead it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, based on your recollection, approximately when was the four hours of direct and indirect fire that the BBC reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was during the visit of Lord Ashdown and the Ambassador Brian Donnelly on their -- on their visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you have dates --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think that was about -- about the 27th of September [Realtime transcript read in error "accept"], because Lord Ashdown had carried out a week's long tour of Kosovo with myself and then went back on I think its Monday, the 28th to speak to President Milosevic about the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The transcript is unclear in regards to what month you're references. It's saying the 27th of "accept." Can you please clarify what month that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my recollection, it's September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So in September --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, if I may interject, Your Honour, the problem is between the dates being virtually the same and the months, and that's where these paragraphs have been muddled up when they've been put together, in my humble opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There appears to be a situation report of the 28th of August, though, which is P2553, and we should perhaps have that on the screen as well so that you can refresh your memory of that. It's your own report as I understand it. If it's that one, it seems to be dated differently. Is that 2553?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doesn't think so, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Exhibit 2554, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we're looking for is 2553.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 2553 is on the screen today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- My administration is terrible today. I do apologise. P02554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I noted it as 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Given today, it's probably because I said that. I apologise, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated] and at the discretion of the Court, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Ojdanic team was able to solicit and receive actually much less redacted copy of this document. I have listed it as an attachment to this if it -- if it helps the Court at all. It's much less scratched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does that help at all in identifying when the video evidence was handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my recollection, Your Honour, the brief on the Kosovo situation by Colonel-General Ojdanic to the BAA was on the 27th of August, 1998, as stated in this report.
