And it was at that briefing that I confronted him with the evidence to make it quite certain that we were no longer accepting the view from the Vojska Jugoslavije that they were not involved in joint military operation with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what did that video actually show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It showed a series, if I remember rightly, sir, a series of shots from -- again, if I remember correctly, many instances of where we had -- we had seen and heard firsthand indirect and direct fire, i.e., artillery and tank fire, being used on villages throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who shot the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my assistant, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did it include evidence of artillery fire actually ongoing or was it film of the resultant damage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It showed artillery fire -- I mean, you have to appreciate that you can't get that close to artillery positions for obvious reasons. Having been under artillery fire myself and directed it on many occasions in operations and during this particular occasion, the fire was coming from a battery position in Blace, and it was firing onto villages east -- sorry, west of Suva Reka, which was viewed by Lord Ashdown and Ambassador Donnelly with a BBC team. And you could physically see and hear the shell-fire landing in and amongst the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm confused again, because you dated the visit when Ashdown was in the company of Donnelly as the end of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown made two visits, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact -- I beg your pardon, sir. The exact dates, without referring to documents, I can't be totally certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he with Donnelly on both occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- in some parts, because they went to view the humanitarian situation in the Pagarusa valley concerned with the UNHCR concern over IDPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the second time he's there, it's the BBC that are doing the filming. The first time he's there, your assistant is doing the filming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Carter, that exhausts what I intend ask at the moment. It's a matter for you how you decide to amplify and clarify this evidence. I remain unclear about the content of what was handed to General Ojdanic, if that's of any assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicate that there was a videotape taken by you and your people in regards to the shelling of Suva Reka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There -- there was film taken which was done on this -- on that occasion, if I remember correctly, by the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Is the BBC the only group who took video evidence, that you're aware of, of the shelling of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I can't answer that. I think we were the only people in the area at the time because of the tense situation in -- within Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I can't categorically say we were the only people to see it, but I would suggest we probably were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who was the videographer of the video that you produced to Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my -- my assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Is your assistant part of the BBC or is that two separate events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. My assistant is a warrant officer in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start on August 28 of 1998, approximately. What, if anything, occurred on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, this was when General Ojdanic gave the brief to the Belgrade Attache Association on the 27th, as stated in this report, and I then refuted some of the claims that he made on behalf of the Vojska Jugoslavije that they were not engaged in joint operations with the MUP. And this was based on what I had seen not just on this occasion, and I think that's perhaps where we're getting some -- some muddling of the facts. But throughout the period of the -- the early summer, June, July and August where I had seen several occasions, including Suva Reka, Blace, in the area of Junik, in the area of Ponosevac on the border, throughout the province I had witness the joint operations. And I was making the point to General Ojdanic that the United Kingdom and other countries were not prepared to accept that they were not carrying out very aggressive action in a joint fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On August 28 of 1998, did you produce a tape to Ojdanic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my recollection, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So if the -- was the tape made that day or was it made sometime prior to August 28, 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was -- I'm sorry, ma'am. That was a correlation of several events in the attempt to persuade the Vojska Jugoslavije General Staff that what they were saying to us was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And during this persuasion, when is it that you produced a videotape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was at the end of the meeting, ma'am, when Colonel -- or General Ojdanic had finished with what as I have described here as a very wooden briefing, and really there was from the Vojska Jugoslavije points of view no change in the situation despite being shown evidence to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So on August 28 of 1998, you produced to Ojdanic a videotape of shelling of Suva Reka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of both Suva Reka, ma'am, and of other areas as I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And who was the videographer of the footage of Suva Reka and other areas in which it was viewed the VJ and the MUP acting together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The correlation of evidence was produced by my warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Could you sponsor and say that you had witnessed personally all of the clips that were produced to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you presented on August 28 of 1998 a package to Ojdanic, it was not solely to Suva Reka, but it was to Suva Reka and many other villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the footage showed joint operations in what fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It showed the -- the joint operations between the Vojska Jugoslavije and the MUP formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you showed a video of joint operations between the MUP and the VJ on August 28 of 1998, how did Ojdanic react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've stated in paragraph 50, the general agreed with my operations, but made the comment that "force would be met with force."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At some other point in time, Lord Ashdown has similar conversations with Milosevic. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present at these conversations, so I cannot say that under oath. As I understood from Lord Ashdown, he was going back from Kosovo direct to the residency; and then on, I think, the 28th of September, he had a meeting with President Milosevic and discussed these areas, but I was not present at that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: But you have had indication directly from Lord Ashdown himself that sometime after you met with Ojdanic, he met with Milosevic on the same matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I understand to be correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, the briefing that Ojdanic gave related to VJ and MUP action anyway. That was the subject of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Ojdanic's briefing, Your Honour, was to try and explain why the -- the members of the association who had been down there, and there weren't that many of them, had seen combined operations, excuse me, because the situation had deteriorated, and as I have reported in several of my reports, the Serbian security forces were facing an insurgency problem. And I have no -- I have no problem with -- with recognising that, and I have said so in many reports. General Ojdanic then said that the -- the degree to which the Vojska Jugoslavije was now involved was commensurate with the situation within Kosovo itself; and from a military point of view, one can understand that heavier involvement. The issue or the issue I have highlighted with respect to the Court is the way that this excessive force was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He, though, was giving a reason, was he not, for -- for the VJ and the MUP acting together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He -- yes, sir. He was explaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, basically, the MUP could not hold the situation together with the forces that they had available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your statement, it was put more specifically as being to protect the lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that how he put it, or did he put it the way you just put it that the MUP couldn't hold the situation together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would not admit to that, for obvious reasons. As I mentioned earlier to you, Your Honour, that there were four further tasks that had been given to the Vojska Jugoslavije; one of which was protecting the lines of communication within Kosovo; secondly, the defence of their barracks where the Pristina Corps were -- were living; thirdly, deployment areas; and I think fourthly, reacting to insurgent activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which of these involved joint actions with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the lines of communication where they would -- they would hold key geographical features to ensure the safety of convoys, and also the -- the attacks on various places that I've indicated, like Junik, Ponosevac, and Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the last part of what was paragraph 50 of your statement explained that you pointed out observing four hours of fire. Now, were you four hours in the one spot observing activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that, according to this, involved fire on Junik, Prilep, Rznic, and Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you would be able, in the one spot, to observe the spread of fire over these areas, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was able to observe that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you able to say anything to Ojdanic about the results of that action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we made a verbal -- when he disclosed that Vojska Jugoslavije now had four additional tasks, we said, "Fine, we accept that. We understand it from a military standpoint of view. What we don't accept is the massive destruction that has gone on throughout the province of Kosovo during the summer months." And this was surely not in the best interests of trying to solve the -- the insurgent terrorist problem within Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "additional tasks," is ensuring the security of their own barracks not an obvious task for the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very obvious task, Your Honour. But respect to the Vojska Jugoslavije, we're dealing with people who -- with an army that has very specific tasks in mind. And it was the constitutional endeavour that they would have obviously defence of their barracks as their prime task, the primary of operations within an internal situation was given to the MUP. The Vojska Jugoslavije was primarily for international boundary security for the sovereign state of the former Yugoslavia. So that -- that is where a fundamental change had come in to deploying across the area, which makes perfect military sense. I don't have a problem with it. We just wanted an understanding that this was also leading to -- or had led to joint operations with huge damage, collateral damage, on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But one of the tasks you mentioned before was that they would protect VJ installations. Now, what do you mean by "VJ installations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the province of Kosovo, Your Honour, there is the 52 Corps, Pristina Corps which had several barrack complexes, which were well known both to ourselves and anyone else. And these, obviously, required protection should the KLA wish to attack these installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in your army, who protects the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- within inside the Ministry of Defence or within the UK, we have primacy within our barracks. Directly outside that primacy is passed to whatever police force the barrack is inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you have a section of your own army which is assigned the duty of ensuring security of the premises with -- from the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being specific, Your Honour, we have the Ministry of Defence police that are deployed around several installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In regard to this use of force that was joint between the MUP and the VJ, what was a standard tactic used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I made clear within this report, ma'am, very often indirect fire would, i.e., fire from artillery or direct fire from tanks, would go into an area in order to warn the local population to move out. Now, whether there was communication between the local population and the security forces as a whole, I can't say. But on most occasions, thankfully, very little human life was lost on this initial frightening of the population, which would then be followed by an assault that in most occasions landed up as a demolition process of businesses and houses and burning of crops and the shooting of farm animals.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Starting with the beginning of your description, you indicated that there was direct and indirect fire, and you said one comes from artillery and the other from tank. But could you further describe what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two ways of bringing -- bringing fire on a potential objective. One is by using the direct fire, either you see line of sight to put it simply from a tank onto a building or objective area, so you can actually see where you're firing at. If the terrain is -- and the terrain, as I've already mentioned, in Kosovo does give you a -- a vision of three to five kilometres and more in certain areas. In other areas, in the more mountainous areas, one of the ways of getting fire into an area is to use indirect, which is either mortars or artillery where there is -- or there should be someone who is looking at the objective and directing the fire into the area that you require it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is the destruction the same, be it direct or indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, most, most of this fire initially was to frighten the inhabitants out of the area, and then there would be direct fire as the forces closed in on villages; for instance, like Malisevo that was completely razed to the ground by a joint MUP/VJ force. I had just driven from Malisevo and met them on the Pec-Pristina road, as I made clear in this report in one of the paragraphs. So I had actually driven from Malisevo and met the force that was about to assault this KLA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If it was a KLA headquarter, wouldn't it be a viable option to level it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have a particular problem with that. But when you start leveling the entire market square -- the headquarters, I know exactly where it was, that is in my humble opinion a genuine target. But then to go and raze the entire village, burn all the shop stalls, wreck all the petrol stations, burn all the crops, and drive all the inhabitants out of it, I would submit that is not the way to win the hearts and minds campaign of the current inhabitants of Malisevo in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, where is that referred to in the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where is which?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the statement, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you referring to Malisevo, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's, Your Honour, paragraph 38, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and 37, Your Honour. This is in the middle of July. In paragraph 37, in the middle, if I may draw your attention to, "Met assault force of SAJ, PJP, and VJ at Cijevo. Ongoing operations in Blace, firing all day... under artillery, tank, and mortar fire from 1.00 onwards. Unanswered question, where is the civilian population from Orahovac." These are --"Malisevo, approximately 30.000 missing." We then found them in the Pagarusa valley." So that is indication of a population being driven out prior to assault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You saw the force amassing, you say, to attack the KLA headquarters in Malisevo. Did you also see the results of this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. I then took, if I remember correctly, the G8 ambassadors down to Malisevo fairly directly after this, to show these senior gentleman the results of such a heavy-handed action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that from this assault 30.000 Albanians were on the move and had gone to the Pagarusa valley. What type of living conditions did these people have once they had their homes levelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, ma'am, they were living under polythane. Some had cars, some had carts, and they were really just tucked under hedge rows a bit like -- with respect to the people concerned, a bit like tramps. They were living in the open air. In the middle of summer, there's not too much of a problem because the temperatures are reasonable, quite hot in fact. But later on in the year, there was concern with the UNHCR that disease and cold could affect the civilian population that was still without proper homes as the weather got colder.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And as these people were living like tramps under hedgerows, what type of food sources or comforts did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had relatively little food, although the amount of food that the Albanians consume is not perhaps as great as what we in the Western world have. So the hardship, and I don't wish to belittle it, they were probably used to a harsher regime than many of us here in this court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the 30.000 that you found in the Pagarusa valley, were there any other large pockets of Albanian civilians that you found without homes living in similar circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Pagarusa valley was probably the major conglomeration in Kosovo. The UNHCR can give you far better detail than I can, but we had indications that there were over 50.000 in Montenegro and other people had gone to Albania and to Macedonia as well. So there was at one stage, I think I'm correct in saying that there were over a million to a million and a half people on the move throughout Kosovo. There was also a collection in the Rogovo -- Rogovo Pass to the west near Pec prior to moving into Montenegro over extremely difficult country, mountainous country.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Throughout your statement you make you make reference to any number of villages multiple times on different dates and assaults against the villages. If they had been levelled, why were the Serbian forces returning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I can't answer that question because the villagers would come back to salvage what they could from the devastated areas; and then on -- on several occasions talking to people, they had been moved out by various contingents whether paramilitary, VJ, or MUP is very difficult to tell because the villagers are extremely frightened. And it was very easy to put into their mouths that they'd been faced by paramilitaries when they could have been faced by people wearing bandannas as an identification between friend and foe with the MUP, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were in Kosovo, did the Serb forces ever bring to your attention atrocities committed upon them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. There was -- and that's a paragraph within this report. When we were staying, as we used to do on many occasions both in Pec and in Djakovica overnight, and we also had a house in Pristina, we were -- we were summoned by the local MUP in Djakovica to go towards a small village area called Glodjane. And that is identified in one of these paragraphs, which might help the Court if we found that first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I point you to paragraph 41, if it assists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes. We had -- we had been out and stayed in the hotel, the Pastrik hotel in Djakovica quite openly. I had actually a red armoured defender in maroon with union jack, so it was clear who I was. There was no subterfuge at all. We were then asked to accompany the MUP to go down to an area in a village called -- a small village called Glodjane, where when we got there we were shown six to eight bodies in a drain, concrete drain. There were bullet scratches on the far bank that indicated that some firing had taken place, and the bodies were in the water. Now, I'm not a pathologist and we were not allowed to closely inspect these bodies, but my advice to the MUP was that they should get proper forensic information so that this incident could be clarified as a war crime for future reference. Now, whether the -- the Serbian authorities did that, I do not know. So I can't say for certain that these bodies were Serb. There were just six to eight bodies in various states of decomposition in this concrete water flow.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As you're seeing six to eight bodies that are alleged by the Serbian forces to be Serbian, did you see anything else more concerning during that trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. What was disturbing was that despite the fact that we'd been escorted in in our own vehicles, this was both the American defence attache and myself, we came across troops, as I indicate in paragraph 41, that were still in the business of burning and looting and razing the villages en route to Glodjane and were perfectly unconcerned that they were doing it in front of two defence attaches.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: These villages on the way to Glodjane, were they KLA Wasp nests, or what viable reason could there have been to level these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area was a known KLA stronghold under the command of Ramush Haradinaj and had caused and continued to cause the Serbian security forces considerable problems; that's sniping and ambushing against the main Pec-Decani-Pristina -- sorry, Djakovica road that was a main supply route for the western side of the element and the Serbian forces concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for the Court how many KLA soldiers were at issue under Ramush Haradinaj's regimen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a difficult question to be precise. I visited his headquarters in and around this area I think twice, and I saw between 20 and 30 personnel who wearing a uniform of some description. Whether that means that they were actually hard-core KLA UCK, I think is open to debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you find a suitable place to interrupt, please, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll ask one final question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you have 30 veteran Haradinaj's KLA force. Can you approximate for the Court how many civilians were damaged in the course of this action?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless there's a foundation for it, I think this is cause for speculation, and it also misstates the testimony. He said there were 30 personnel wearing a uniform. He did not say they were veteran Haradinaj's KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems a very general question for a start, but it must be very difficult for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the Ramush's area when we went to visit - and would I say this as -- as a general application throughout Kosovo whenever we went to various KLA headquarters, and if there were important people coming like an ambassador or Deputy Head of Mission or whatever - inevitably there would be more "KLA personnel" turning up to give, in my opinion, an overstated version of how many KLA were within the combat, if you will, the insurgent area. And that's why I make it quite clear there may have been 20 or 30 there in uniform, but purely or possibly for show. There were definitely ten to 15 who were armed and who were providing some kind of perimeter defence around Haradinaj's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I think the implication that was being made by Mr. Lukic is there could have been more un-uniformed personnel in that area. Is that likely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that's a reasonable statement, but we're getting into surmising [Realtime transcript read in error "surprising"], if I may be so bold, as to the numbers. I have made a comment, Your Honour, on what I -- what I reckon to be what I have called the hard-core element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've also departed from the question which caused the controversy, and that's probably just as well. If you do intend to pursue that line, you need to establish a foundation for it. So we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, 77, line 21 he said "surmising" and not "surprising," and I think that's an important difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it was "surmising."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll need to break again, so we'll go into closed session for you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I had alike to move on to the part of your statement which involves deals command issues beginning at paragraph 47. In it you indicate that there must have been a coordination centre, presumably in Pristina. Can you elaborate a bit further on why you believe that must have been the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on the -- based on my experience around the world in counter-insurgency operations, I would have find it very difficult not to have thought there would be a coordination centre between the various elements of the forces deployed in Kosovo and in this case the VJ and the MUP, to prevent, as I said in the paragraph, what is now called blue-on-blue operations, forces firing on one another by mistake, and other areas of issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your time within Kosovo, did you ever encounter any sort of blue-on-blue activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that we did, ma'am, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Given that you had military police, reservists, paramilitaries, and civilians active at different times within Kosovo during 1998 and 1999, what would you have expected to have seen without a coordination centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. I don't think he's -- I don't think she laid down a foundation for his knowledge in 1999, in particularly relevant portions thereof, since we know the witness was not stationed on the ground there during that time period. So without that foundation, I think this question is bordering on being improper.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, his statement very clearly states that he was in Kosovo almost until the bombing campaign began in March of 1999, so can clearly speak at least to the first quarter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a foundation for the witness to answer that question, both in his experience within Kosovo itself during 1998 and 1999 and also his general experience of counter-insurgency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If -- if there had not been a coordination centre within Pristina, then I would have expected serious coordination issues between the various forces concerned. The fact that -- as far as I know, there was no clashes between the forces, although you must understand that some of these attacks took place when I was not present in the area. So whether there were blue-on-blue, I can't answer that question. But I would very surprised to hear that there had not been a coordination centre from purely a command and control purpose from the - I beg your pardon, madam - from the field commander back to his military and political commanders back in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you say "a coordination centre," what are you imagining with that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, it would have been a mixed headquarters with representation from all the forces deployed within Kosovo and with a -- both a political and military mix to ensure that the political will was being followed by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on what you were seeing within Kosovo as well as your interactions with some of the high-level personalities within Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, what do you believe was the -- the level of order? Who -- did all of these branches exist equally, or do you feel that there was some sort of pecking order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect that the -- the MUP, who had primacy for an internal situation as this insurgency, was would presumably be running it, maybe in a dual capacity with the various Vojska Jugoslavije generals within the Pristina Corps and 3rd Army based in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What about what you saw in Kosovo led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I would have found it very unusual not to have had a -- a mixed or a dual coordination centre within Kosovo to prevent unnecessary casualties between their own forces and to ensure presumably some kind of continuity in the -- in the various actions that took place, and that would have both a political and a military -- a military side depending on how the -- the politicians wished to -- the military to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. You also indicated in one of your previous answers that you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I have no intention of interfering with Ms. Carter's way of examining. When you say whether it was in 1998 or 1999, I wanted to warn you against a couple of things. We have to make a distinction. In 1999, there was the peacetime, the peaceful period, and the period of NATO invention; then in 1998, which is very familiar to the witness, it seems, there was a part of it as well as a part in 1999 when the witness was absent. Therefore, please could you ask specific questions referencing to a specific period and area. Otherwise, if we merge all of those together, it doesn't amount to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have no doubt that Ms. Carter is conscious of the need to confine the witness's answers to the periods that he has experience of, and indeed he's been conscious of that himself in the answers he's given by pointing out that certain events took place when he wasn't present. So we are alert to the point. Thank you, Mr. Fila. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When do you believe such a coordination centre would have been established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That, I think, leads to my intervention. I was going to intervene earlier. The questions that you are addressing just now, appear to me to be matters of expertise that you would expect to be asked of an expert witness who might draw conclusions from a whole series of factors. Insofar as this witness is concerned, then what you're asking for is speculation, and you've already had a measure of speculation in his answer. That's no fault -- that's no criticism of the witness. He's been forced into that situation. But he's not a person who has prepared himself to come here to give expert evidence based on a full study of all the materials relating to events in Kosovo that might point to a coordination body.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then I'll move along to paragraph 54 of your statement and as well as a comment that you had made earlier in regard to General Pavkovic's involvement in Kosovo. What has led you to believe that General Pavkovic has been acting outside the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've stated in paragraph 54 of this report, we had a meeting with General Dimitrijevic with whom I'd met on several occasions during the -- the whole of the year of 1998; and on this particular one, on the 5th of November, as is stated here, he said he was extremely worried about the situation within Kosovo and that General Pavkovic appeared to be working outside the loop of command. He made statements to me then, and I think at other times as well, that he and General Perisic were no longer now within the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Based on what you were viewing in the field and based on your relationships with these two individuals, how much credence did you put in their concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I placed a great deal of credence within it, because both of them. General Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff and had been for a number of years, and General Dimitrijevic was Chief for Counter-intelligence and therefore I would -- I would entertain that he was a key player within the overall command and control and coordination of operations against an insurgency. I mean, head of -- head of a counter-intelligence should be leading in the intelligence evaluation against an insurgency as was happening in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it appears the witness has only answered half of the question. He was also asked to say what it was based on his -- what he was viewing in the field that gave him credence to this, and he didn't respond to that part, and I think he should. I would like to know what he was viewing in the field that made him believe there was credence in those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, can you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only repeat, Your Honour, that when these interviews took place with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, these were what they stated to me. I don't -- I cannot collaborate that any further than that. I just find it very strange that the head of the -- Chief of the General Staff, the head of the Vojska Jugoslavije, and the Chief of Counter-intelligence should tell a defence attache that they're not in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely clear, and it's clear from your statement that you were told that. You've now confirmed what I don't think I was aware of before, that you actually spoke to Perisic about this. Was that on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Your Honour, that was on about a couple of occasions, and the same with General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I've made the same note myself in reading your statement before, as has now been raised both by Ms. Carter and Mr. Ackerman. Were there any signs you can identify on the ground independently of what you had been told that would confirm that somehow or other the chain of command that should be observed was not being observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the -- the personal meetings between myself and these very two very senior generals, and they them -- they themselves stating that the situation appeared to be getting out of -- of control in Kosovo and that General Pavkovic was in name was reporting direct to Mr. Milosevic, no, I can't specifically say other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think the fact that we were raising -- sorry, if I may, Your Honour. We were raising concern about the level of violence being dished out by the VJ and the MUP and these two officers, General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, were concerned but were unable to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Counsel would be accused of asking a leading question if they said what I am about to say, but is that not an answer to the question, in fact, that things that you observed were getting out of hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- in my opinion, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Beginning in January of 1998 and progressing through the year, what specifically was becoming more egregious that you would indicate that it was "getting out of hand"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you asking for something that we haven't already heard? Or have we not spent the morning listening to that? If Mr. Crosland thinks he can supplement rather than repeat what he has said already, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I think if Ms. Carter is referring to the Racak incident, then that was probably a fundamental moment when the -- the Racak incident in mid-January --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I interrupt? That's certainly -- that's certainly not responsive to the question, because the question is about January 1998 and progressing through the year; in other words, 1998. Racak was in 1999. So she wasn't asking about that, and I don't think the witness should simply volunteer testimony that he thinks might be interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That does seem a fair comment. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Actually, going more towards the end of 1998, I'll direct you to December of 1998 and some of the actions that were taking place then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to wait until you've concluded with paragraph 54, but then I wanted to warn you against something which is unclear. It begins with, "On the day of the 5th of October," whereas in the transcript we have the 5th of November. That should be corrected. I wanted to wait for Ms. Carter to finish to intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the error in the transcript, Mr. Fila, which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 54. It says the 5th of November, whereas, the transcript says the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page in the transcript though?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've passed that point because I waited for Ms. Carter to finish so as not to interrupt. I wanted to be gentlemanly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can somebody help me with the page and line?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 83. Yes. If you look at paragraph 54 of your statement, you'll see there's a date at the beginning. When you were dealing with that, you referred to that date as the 5th of November. Can you tell us which is correct? It says "October" in the statement, and you said "November" in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presume that is a type error, Your Honour, I'm afraid. I can't -- I can't say without looking at the original documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which are you suggesting is the type error? The one in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the one in the statement, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that should be November. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to bring up the collegium minutes of 25 February 1999, which is at P00941, specifically to page 24. I'm looking to paragraph 4. Your Honour, the Prosecution will be making a submission from the bar table with respect to this document. This is another of the collegium minutes that was tendered on 22 January 2007. It was received pursuant to an RAF in the same fashion as those that have already been admitted, and we're seeking to admit it from the bar table now. I'm looking to page 24, paragraph 4, and specifically in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please review the paragraph that begins, "I can see that we're still settling into a routine," and let me know when you're complete. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you aware of who the commander of the 3rd Army was in February 25th of 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I -- if I were to hold out to you that the author of this statement is Ojdanic, and Ojdanic is indicating that engagements are taking place within the field of which he had not approved, what does that indicate to you with regards to the command and control structure at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this appears to be very, very fragmented if the Chief of the General Staff and the army commander are -- are do two different things, and generally that doesn't lead to very good communication and cooperation between the staff concerned. So I would -- I would be worried with this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why would you be worried?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. You've ruled when General Vasiljevic was here that it was not appropriate for a witness who is not present at a meeting where minutes are taken, is not aware of the context in which it's taken to offer comment on it, and that exactly what's happening here. This witness cannot comment on a lengthy document which are the minutes of a VJ collegium where he was not present, and he does not know what preceded or followed this one paragraph we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, this paragraph lies squarely within the witness's previous testimony. He's indicating that Pavkovic is going out of the chain of command, that there are already issues that he was noting, were having conversations with between Perisic and Dimitrijevic. This is squarely relevant with what he was understanding beginning in 1998 that there is a fracture chain of command, Pavkovic is going outside of the appropriate chain of command, and is making decisions that are not his to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the first place, what he understood was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have a little order here at the moment. I'm aware you're on your feet, Mr. Ackerman, but just hold on for a moment. Now, Ms. Carter, you are asking, "What does that indicate to you with regards to the command and control structure?" That sounds like a question for an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, Colonel Crosland had ongoing communications with General Dimitrijevic. General Dimitrijevic is the person who was making the objection here in the VJ collegium minutes. There has become a question here today in regards to what was happening within Kosovo, as if the statements that Dimitrijevic are making to Colonel Crosland are unfounded or unsupported. And I would argue to the Court that this document and this type of document shows that what Colonel Crosland was learning from the individuals who are privy to these meetings was in fact accurate, and that does place significantly into who is going to be responsible in the field of operation going into 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what this -- this says to any reader that General Ojdanic was taking a decision because he didn't like what had happened. He decided this unit must be used as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, if the document is taken as a whole, there become -- it becomes much clearer that there are two concerns that are being articulated within these collegium minutes. One is the use of this brigade inside of Kosovo as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. We're dealing with one question you have asked in relation to one paragraph. You're not taking it in context. You're asking the witness a question exclusively out of context. So let's deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly, Your Honour. And what I'm anticipating -- or what I'm trying to elicit is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't tell the witness what you're about to -- should I ask him to leave if you really find this very important, because perhaps he should. What you're telling me is that I can't read this and make -- and properly understand it and I need his expertise. Now, he's not here as an expert witness. He's here to tell us what he experienced, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, based on your previous rulings with regard to these specific documents, you indicated that while you felt that the documents were authentic and they were appropriate for admittance, what you were concerned was how much weight that you to give to them. What I'm trying to elicit from this witness is what he is learning in Kosovo at the time is cooperating --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, I wish she wouldn't say in front of the witness what it is she would trying to elicit. You just told her not to do it, and now she is doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to leave the courtroom while we deal with this, so we'll go into closed session to enable you to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, your question is confined to something the witness can glean from this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, what the Prosecution is attempting to do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What the Prosecution is attempting to do is merely show what weight can be given to these documents, that these documents are not taken in isolation, that there are other witnesses that can corroborate these type of meetings and these type of concerns. Colonel Crosland has been very clear that he indicated there was a chain of command that was being circumvented that was going from General Pavkovic through Milosevic to Sainovic. What this document shows is exactly what was being -- what the concern was by Dimitrijevic, that Pavkovic is not taking order along the chain of command but, rather, going outside of that chain of command and making decisions on his own. So the attempt isn't to make -- have the witness necessarily contribute in regards to being able to say that there is -- that he can speak any further to the chain of command itself but, rather, that the Court can have weight to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in an ideal world, what's the answer to the question you've asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All the -- the only thing I'm expecting the witness to answer is that Dimitrijevic told him beginning in 1998 that Pavkovic was circumventing the chain of command, and that this is showing in February of 1999 indicates that that is precisely what's happening, that what he's learning from Dimitrijevic is supported within the VJ collegium minutes. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that not obvious from the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, the Prosecution is merely -- is merely attempting to follow the order of the Court. The Court was very clear when admitting the previous documents on the 22nd that it wanted weight, that it somehow wanted corroboration; and that -- that is what we're attempting to do is merely support the documents as opposed to the document necessarily supporting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me page reference for this expression of will on the part of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The argument is broken in two. It starts on page 8807 where the Court originally admits the documents; then there is a series of arguments on behalf of Mr. Petrovic with regards to these documents. I do apologise. The paragraph where it's -- I was having that reading from the Court indicates from you these two documents are also including the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page? Or 8809; right? Yes, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, 8809, beginning at 01, that there -- it appears that you're only accepting the documents to the extent that they are being addressed in evidence. There are some other statements that are going to be made throughout Mr. Vasiljevic's testimony, such as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Vasiljevic was being used, and I probably offensively at one stage described him as a puppet. That was no criticism of him; it was criticism of what the Prosecution were doing. They were using him to read something out. That's not what you're doing here. You're doing something different, which I you may be entitled to do. I don't think Mr. O'Sullivan is right to compare the two situations. You're asking a man with personal experiences on the ground to say is consistent with a document. Let's hear what the other objections are. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been trying to think of a term that might describe this, and I think I'll use grasping at straws. The Chamber will recall that everything that everything that this witness has said about Pavkovic going outside the complain of command was information that came from Perisic and Dimitrijevic in 1998. There's nothing in the record that says that Pavkovic was going outside the chain of command in 1999. It all has to do with 1998. This witness has no knowledge of what was going on in 1999, at least from a personal standpoint. You'll also remember, Your Honours, that it is the theory of the Prosecution that Perisic was replaced because he would not do the bidding of the Milosevic people and was replaced with Ojdanic, who would. And now they're saying that you should also look at this to show that -- that Pavkovic was also continuing to go outside the chain of command even after these replacements had been made that were supposed to solve that problem. And finally, and I think most importantly in some ways, the question that she asked is the second one I know for sure today that is extraordinarily misleading. She says,"If I were to hold out to you that author of this statement is Ojdanic, and Ojdanic is indicating that engagements are taking place within the field of which he has not approved." That is not in there. There is nothing about engagements taking place in the field that he has not approved. And the engagements take place in the field all the time, and this witness will tell you this, that aren't approved by the chief of General Staff. The Chief of the General Staff is not a micro-manager, and so engagements go on all the time in the field that he doesn't approve of. The local commander has a great deal of authority to deal with issues as they come up within the general orders that he has. So that -- that question is misleading. It misled the witness, I suspect, and she should not be asking misleading questions. She can say to the witness, "Please read that and tell us if you have any conclusions about it," if the witness is an expert witness, which he isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to point to the fact that Ms. Carter said that the witness mentioned that General Pavkovic through Milosevic reported to Sainovic; and in his testimony, the witness has never mentioned the name Sainovic so far. And I'm talking about line 91, page -- sorry, page 91, line 21. That exists in the statement, but it was not mentioned in the testimony, and he didn't say it in the way Mr. -- Ms. Carter put it. Pavkovic reported to Milosevic and Milosevic reported to Sainovic. That's not the way it was. Look at the line 20, 21 on page 91. He never mentioned Sainovic at all. He -- and he has to be asked whether he wants to mention this particular name or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We agree with Mr. Ackerman's submission that this question proceeds on a false premise, an inaccurate statement of the evidence on which it purports to be based. However, we don't accept that the witness can't relate events in 1999 to his own experience earlier, and we do not see any reason why the Prosecution should not present him with a set of circumstances, for example, what's said in the paragraph referred to, and ask him how that compares with what he had been told by Dimitrijevic was actually happening. That's a matter of clarification of the factual evidence that he's actually giving. Now, let's have the witness back, please. We need closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, we've sustained the objection that that question so you will not answer it, but we are trusting Ms. Carter to ask another question which will keep everyone in the courtroom firmly stuck to their seats. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in reference to the paragraph that you've just reviewed, how does that compare to what you have been told by Dimitrijevic in regards to what was actually happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was down in Kosovo in March 1999 on very nearly my last tour into the area, I found two units, probably the 211 from Nis and possibly the 37. The Nis one was in Kursumlija Banja, which is a forward deployment area for 3rd Army, along with 1st Armoured Brigade from Belgrade. I also found another unit which may well be the 37th - I did not identify it at the time in Raska - which seemed to me to indicate that this is a huge amount of force to bring into an area that already had 13.000 troops and about 10.000 MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I don't think is an answer to the question that was asked, because that could have happened because General Ojdanic ordered it for all we know, or approved it. But the question you're being asked is how the information you were getting from Dimitrijevic about orders passing out with the normal chain of command compares with or how it matches up to the events that are disclosed in the paragraph that you read in this minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it -- it reinforces and confirms what General Dimitrijevic said to me that the chain of command had -- had been fractured and Pavkovic was reporting direct to Milosevic, bypassing the then chief of the General staff and the Chief of Counter-intelligence. I can't comment any further on that. They made that statement to me. I put it into a report that is submitted under oath. I don't think I can add anything further to it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have one further objection that I need to make. If -- if the Chamber doesn't know, the Chamber will know very soon that it was -- it was in early January, I think around the 12th of January, that General Pavkovic became commander of the 3rd Army. This has no date as to when it was that the proposal came from the commander of the 3rd Army, and it could have come before that change, it could have come after. But until there is a date known regarding that proposal, I don't think General Pavkovic can be put into that mix because it may have come from General Samardzic instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I now ask to bring up P2166, beginning of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in regards to paragraph 60 of your statement, you had reviewed this document during your interview session in October of 2006. You began taking issue with it within paragraph 60, but we would ask you to further explain what is your concern with regards to the numbers being depicted as well as the actions being provided for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In essence, the numbers depicted here appear extremely high to me, and the suggestion that many, many Albanians are being killed, I would ask well, where are these bodies and what proof have we got of this? And I think that the -- the estimate of 12.000 terrorists and 8.000 manoeuvre terrorists I find extraordinary; and the strongest terrorist forces in paragraph 2, again I find it extraordinary these figures are being produced. Based on what evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You have indicated previously to the Court that you believe there were approximately 400 hard-core fighters, but that seems to leave room for some other qualifications to be named within the KLA. What -- what are the total numbers, fighters, supports, the people that you believe are actually assisting the KLA in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I would stick with the low hundreds of actual hard-core fighters, because the situation was getting quite serious in 1998 as the Serbs were building up a head of steam in their counter-insurgency operations. To try and answer the question as say how many people were actively supporting the Kosovo Liberation Army, I think that's very difficult to put an accurate figure at. It could number a couple of -- 3.000 depending on -- and that may be well out of fear to support the KLA because the KLA were based in or around their villages or their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me, Ms. Carter, what was the figure the Chief of Staff of the KLA gave us? 17.000, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 17.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has presented a witness from the KLA here, and they haven't challenged. They have presented as their witness, with 17.000 men in the KLA, not the -- not the people running food back and forward for them and supporting them with shelter and so forth. Now, what we're getting not just from you but from others in not dissimilar positions to you is a completely different picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour, entirely. And I would stick by my number of the low hundreds -- sorry, are we going -- based on what one so in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can understand the KLA pretending at the time that they had very large numbers, but there seems little point now in a witness coming here and telling us that they had these numbers at that time, if it's -- if it's quite untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it -- and the only people who can really answer that, Your Honour, is the KLA themselves, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But as the successful conclusion to this campaign drew to a close, then more and more people appeared on the KLA side for very obvious reasons. Because if you weren't part of the force that fought for Kosovo, I would suggest you were going to lose out in the future of -- of this province. But whether that means these people were hard-core terrorists, I would -- I would doubt, myself. But you're quite right, sir, there was a huge increase in numbers. But I don't think at this level at this time. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's then much more like a freedom fighting army, of course, than a terrorist organisation, if it's given these numbers and a rather militaristic complexion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you are well aware, Your Honour, it changed the Kosovo Protection Corps very quickly after we came back in with the ACE Rapid Reaction Corps in 1999, and I was part of that ACE Rapid Reaction Corps that came back in. And so there were an awful lot more KLA on the ground then that there ever had been in my experience prior to then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now move to page 4, both in the numeral 5 at the top of the page as well as numeral 7 in regard to the bottom of the page. What comments do you have on the Serbian assistance to the thousands of people that you saw in places like the Pagarusa valley? Was this assistance actually being found by the -- the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The -- the shelter and provision was done by the various non-governmental organisations primarily led by UNHCR and other organisations which may or may not have had -- I mean, there were some Serbian non-governmental organisations involved. I think Mother Teresa was one. But the majority were external organisations that came in to try -- to try and provide shelter for the many thousands of people who were out in displaced areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now move to page 5, specifically this seventh portion in regards to the combat operations. You expressed some concern previously in regards to those numbers as well. Can you explain to the Court why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in paragraph -- on the seventh paragraph in saying the plan was implemented, the terrorist forces losses from various reasons were 32.594; and terrorists up to 36, 30th of September. I don't understand that. In the course of conducting combat operations, 3.500 terrorists were killed, 5 to 6.000 were wounded, eight and half to nine and a half were put out of action. I don't know understand what means. Four to 5.000 fled Kosovo and Metohija. That's fair enough. Six to 6.500 threw down their weapons, 560 were liquidated by the State Security Service. I would suggest that someone needs to answer. "Liquidation" is a pretty final statement. And then in the following paragraph, a total of 1.344 terrorists were put out of action. I don't understand that what means. It then breaks it down, I suppose. Six hundred and sixty-six liquidated. Again, who is responsible for that. Eight hundred and fifty-six wounded, 822 captured. Where are these people? And pack animals were liquidated in the same area. I think there are a lot of questions in there that need to be answered by the responsible people in charge of operations, and that's the RDB and the VJ and the MUP who were presumably controlling these operations. But we certainly didn't see anywhere near or find the bodies to provide a body count of these proportions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With regards to those who were captured, were you ever privy to any sort of prisons or any of these captured fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There -- there were instances early on in the Drenica at Ferronikli plant at Gllogoc, which we attempted to approach fairly in, I think in March, April time. We were physically prevented by security forces going there. I went into the prison at Istok after the war and found two KLA fighters in there and a whole load of documents that were "licna kartas" that appeared to have written on it "To be killed." Now, whether this was carried out or not, I don't know. There were indications within --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the building that was also bombed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are yet again expanding this indictment going into areas that this Trial Chamber has ruled do not apply to these proceedings. I think it's improper, and it causes a great hardship for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that's been asked though relates to whether the witness had encountered any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this part of his answer is non-responsive to his question, and it's bringing us into an area where we're going to have to reopen a whole bunch of areas that we had thought we wouldn't have to and that will affect preparations for the Defence cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, without tipping my hand to the witness in regards to what the follow-up question is going to be, I certainly don't want to delve into the Dubrava prison issues per se, but there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're now at the stage where you should pose the next question, and we'll hear if there is an objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So when you see this number who have been captured yet you are not-- you're not locating persons that -- that meet those numbers and you also are seeing a number of people "liquidated," under normal counter-insurgency, counter-terrorism tactics, is that an appropriate action to take even against KLA fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, do not answer that question. I actually don't understand the question you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is an objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, but the part I did understand sure sounded like she was asking for this witness to become an expert again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems that way to me, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court had indicated on page 31 at line 10 that this -- this witness, because of his long 37 years of counter-insurgency experience all over the world, has become somewhat of a quasi-expert. He can certainly indicate what the protocol has been in the field of operations as he's been involved in with regards to counter-insurgency, and so we would just urge the Court to it allow the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. This is a matter of expertise. This is not the appropriate witness to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll move along, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when -- I'm going to direct you now to page 7, number 4 in the middle of the page, which is making reference to 12.500 reservists already being called up in 1998. How does that fit into the number of forces that you saw in Kosovo and what would be appropriate for the level of the KLA problem in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bear in mind that this is a question of police reservists, is that something you had personal knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we had, because we made an assessment starting from very early on in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still have an objection though, because the first part of the question I think is okay. The second part is again asking for an opinion and for him to opine on the level of an expert, which I think improper for him to say what level would be appropriate for the KLA problem in Kosovo. That's asking for an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, one has to take the numbers into account. The witness has already articulated the number of VJ forces, the number of MUP forces versus the 400 KLA fighters. I'm just trying to elicit what does 12.500 additional forces of the FRY and Serbia do to that figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the first part -- that's the first part of your question which Mr. Ivetic concedes is okay. It's the second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I add that this document purports to talk about training, not utilisation in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, just hold on, please. So you should break this down. You can ask the first part. I find it difficult to see really what the second part is aiming at, but bearing in mind that there were agreements about the level of troops that should be present in the area anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, with regards to the 12.500 reservists that are listed within this document, how does that fit into the number of forces that you saw in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the entire period, there were -- the MUP numbers fluctuated between 8 and 10 to 12.000 depending on the activities that were going on. It would be quite natural towards the end of an operation that started early March for reservists to be called up in order for these units to have what we call "reauxmont" [phoen] and to have time off to go back to their families and have a normal life. So I don't see the figure as being out of the way as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, lastly, I'd move to page 10, the middle of the page where it indicates that approximately 48.000 guns were distributed to the local population. Again, how does that fit in with the figures that you were seeing on the ground in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, bearing in mind that the Balkans is a gun-carrying culture, there are plenty of weapons flying around which came out of Albania when Albania went bust in 1977 -- 1997, rather, I wouldn't necessarily disagree with that figure. It maybe little high, but there were plenty of these weapons about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Now moving within your statement to the period preceding pre-NATO bombing, that begins at paragraph 68. You indicated that there are three brigades that entered Kosovo during the lead-up into the NATO bombing in 1999. How did three brigades enter Kosovo without the internationals noticing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the Serbian security forces had learnt quite a lot of lessons and that with the possible onset of the NATO bombing that had been made quite clearly plain in the ACTORD issued by General Clark from SACEUR, from NATO, that they had started to move in in small packets units into the operational area. And I would give them 10 out of 10 for doing this in a clear and opportune way, because they probably realised that there was an inevitability that NATO would eventually end up bombing Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So once you add these three additional brigades, what are the forces we're looking at in Kosovo in 1999 during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're looking at -- at approximately with the forces already in Kosovo of 12.000 with an extra three brigades something up to about 15.000 I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask the Court to pull up P940, the collegium minutes of 21 February, 1999, looking to page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would you expect additional troops to be able to do to combat NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a very good question. And the reason I -- I believe that the Serbian security forces moved in extra troops is because their method of operation or method of operandus was static, as opposed to mobile defence. And what they would do was to drive tanks and other vehicles into houses that would then settle around them. The tanks would go cold and it is extremely difficult to pick out any vehicles as NATO found out during its bombing campaign. Therefore, the Serbs were quite rightly playing to their strength because they were not, and realized knew they could not, outfight NATO if it came to a mobile battle. So it was good strategic sense to have moved in, in small packets, these forces, to allow them to get settled in and to go quiet before NATO's, as I said, more inevitably the bombing came closer. So I think this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that in anticipation of a ground invasion later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why else would it be? This is actually quite an important issue, I think here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've -- I've just indicated, Your Honour, that the Serbian -- the Vojska Jugoslavije, primarily, was not designed to fight a mobile battle. It not have the command and control structures that NATO would have had and the firepower from air that NATO could have deployed against it with helicopters, armed helicopters, and the -- the vast array of NATO Air Forces that were, in fact, used in the bombing campaign against Kosovo and Serbia itself. Therefore, they were putting in position static defence, which did not rely on a lot of resupply because they resupplied locally.
