And I think, if I may suggest, we have to understand that the Serbian Vojska Jugoslavije was not as sophisticated, and I don't mean that as a slur on them. I mean that as a genuine comment that they would be able to maintain themselves in positions far better than more sophisticated forces that require replenishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that your mind is turning to fighting an invading force rather than a bombing force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, I think they were looking at both options. They couldn't do anything about the bombing, because they had -- they had then excellent air defence assets which also went cold. And they went cold for the quite simple reason is that they could not strike top grade aircraft at 60.000 feet. All you did was give a signal as to where to fire a missile down the beam to that air defence position. Therefore, they were playing to their strengths and forcing NATO, if it had to, to have fought mobile battle which inevitably would have meant a lot more casualties on both sides. So I think, in my opinion, it was good planning on behalf of the Vojska Jugoslavije.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up a bit, actually moving you through your statement to paragraphs 72 through 74 in which you indicate that you believe there was a design for a mass movement of the Albanians out of Kosovo. How does your belief that there was a plan, in fact, to eject the Albanians from Kosovo play into the mass numbers that were already in place in these three additional brigades, if at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think with respect the only people that can answer that is probably the Vojska Jugoslavije. But having identified three extra brigade units in an area that already had a surplus of troops, I -- one could only draw the conclusion that there was speculation that -- that a clearance or cleansing operation was about to commit, and bearing in mind that we're -- we're right on the date that NATO bombing started. So I think these additional forces were asked for in order to possibly carry out a cleansing operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why do you believe there's a cleansing operation at issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I don't -- I don't actually understand why you need another three brigades when you've already got more than adequate troops to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of them bringing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on, I'm puzzled now that you didn't answer my question this way. It was good strategic sense, you say, to have moved in in small packs these forces to allow them to get settled in and go quiet before NATO, as I said more inevitably the bombing came closer. So that suggested, I understood from your answers to me, that you were commending them for military wisdom in what they had done. And as I was trying to understand that, and I was I have to say having difficulty understanding it, unless it was to repel an invading force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But now you're giving a different answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I think the fact that these forces had been moved down in small packets and had -- and had defeated NATO surveillance, that is commendable on the Serbian -- on the VJ's part. The fact that they needed or they thought they needed more troops in Kosovo, perhaps they feared a NATO land invasion. I don't know. I was not the NATO planner, obviously; therefore, if they wish to put the numbers higher in order to perhaps convince NATO that a land operation was not the correct operation to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm now understanding you to be saying that the real reason for these extra brigades was to carry out an ethnic cleansing operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. It might have been. There was indications from various signal intelligence that this was one of the factors that could come into play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to pull up P01968.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document I understand has not been admitted, and therefore not been authenticated. It has no signatures, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We were told earlier this one has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was admitted on 23 November, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what the document indicates, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the one that hadn't been was 1969, which perhaps we've yet to come to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you've reviewed this Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija order to supply support to MUP in the Drenica sector. I point you to the first page in regards to who the enemy is or is claimed to be on March 24, 1999. Does this meet with what you were viewing in Kosovo shortly before this bombing, four days before this bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the Drenica was a continual battle area through 1998 and 1999 and was considered one of the -- the premier KLA operational areas just west of Kosovo. So, again, the figures, I can't -- or as stated there, they seem high to me, but that's what presumably some intelligence has put together. The villages that they're referring to are all well-known KLA villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll move you to the second page to the bottom where it's the task of the Pristina Corps, where it indicates, "The Pristina Corps with reinforcements and the armed non-Siptar population in KIM shall support MUP forces in defeating and destroys the STS in the zone of responsibility." Based on your indications previously that you had intelligence that there was a concern for the Albanians in this area, what does it indicate to you when you're seeing an order tasking the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presume they mean by this the civilian Serbs who were armed, but as I said already these people were armed fairly lightly. But it makes very little difference in the amount of MUP and VJ that was already available to -- to do a clearing operation of this type. But the wording is -- is pretty drastic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the purpose of bringing in the three extra brigades and other activities of the forces of FRY and Serbia leading up to the bombing campaign is to deal with the concerns of a NATO bombing strike or a future possibility that there's going to be a ground invasion, why would you start making differentiations between the Albanian population and the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that -- that question. The premise is -- doesn't follow from the evidence we've heard. It's calling for absolute speculation and conjecture on this witness's part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, the witness in his statement, beginning at paragraph 72, begins indicating that there are the belief the international community at the time that there were plans for the VJ and the MUP to start serious moves against the population of Kosovo and specifically the Albanian population, when their -- when the non-Siptar population is being tasked but leaving the Albanians to hang. I think -- I believe, Your Honour, this witness can comment to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think she's now led the witness with what she wants him to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Crosland, of the extent to which the authorities could count on Kosovo Albanians standing up and swearing an oath of allegiance to Serbia and fighting in the Serbian forces? Is that something within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think by now you would have of got many Kosovo Albanians doing that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I mean, it's one of these questions that unless you're bringing an expert to tell us about this, Mr. Crosland's no better placed to answer it than I am, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I would say, Your Honour, if you may permit me, is there was concern that there be some kind cleansing operation, and this was from signal intelligence during the period before the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but that becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. If your intelligence says that there is a going to be an ethnic cleansing operation against Albanians and then someone says we're arming the non-Siptar population, then it's easy to put two and two together. On the other hand, there might be an equally good reason for not even dreaming about arming the Albanian population which is quite unrelated to ethnic cleansing. And all I'm saying is you're probably not in any better position than most of us, from what we've heard, to judge that. You're not coming here as an expert who has carried out a survey of Albanian loyalty to the Yugoslav army at that time. So I find that any answer you give would not assist me at all in trying to reach any conclusions here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So with your -- with your involvement with the Serbian leadership, had you ever had conversations in regards to whether their actions were deemed offensive or defensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see how the -- the amount of damage and destruction that was caused throughout Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 can deem -- can be deemed otherwise than destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ackerman, that the question is a prelude to seeking specific information, because it otherwise doesn't help us either. Are you going to go to specific occasions when that -- that subject was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And there is an exhibit based on some of the answers I may show this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you're still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I -- you may have responded to my objection already. The -- the question asks for conversations he had with the leadership, and he hasn't answered whether he had any such conversations or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know there have been some, but I was hoping that this was going to lead to specific evidence of exchanges which might indicate the transfer of specific information. Is that where we're going?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct you initially to the conversation that you indicated you had with Ojdanic in regards to his concept of force would be met with force. You've certainly explored your belief that there was a disproportionate force, but have you had any other conversations with any of the Serb leadership or privy to any intelligence with regards to the Serb leadership in regards to how they viewed their use of force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think throughout the 1998 and 1999, in various conversations with particularly General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, one continually raised the point that whilst accepting there was an insurgency or terrorist movement in Kosovo and Metohija, the appropriate force was not being used or the disproportionate was being used in order to -- to clear this problem. And that is down in many reports. The damage that was done throughout the Kosovo -- the province of Kosovo to both normal villages, towns, marketplaces in both Pec, Decani, Djakovica, Urosevac, the hundreds of villages I've indicated that were wrecked, burnt, crops that were left in flames, and livestock that was wantonly shot. I think all of that implies that a huge amount of disproportionate force was -- was created in an attempt to halt, as I've said, an insurgency that was a -- a thorn in the side of the Serbians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are these many reports, Ms. Carter, exhibits in the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Not as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's beginning to look like Ms. Carter is trying to figure out how many different ways she can ask a question that will elicit exactly the same answer. The answer we just got to that question was an answer we've had about six times today, and you indicated to her that you expect she was going to talk about conversations about the Serb view of things. And she said that's where she was going, and we get to this again and this is like the sixth time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, that is the question I've asked and I would like to re-urge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What from the Serbian perspective did you have any conversations in regards to their belief of the activities? Were they offensive or defensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their initial reaction was that these were defensive actions until we proved that they were offensive by the amount of damage that had been done, but that was not accepted by General Ojdanic until he was shown video footage of various actions being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did the rules of engagement of the Serb forces after you confronted Ojdanic change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the rules of engagement for the Serbian forces were. I can't answer that question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Either while you were in Kosovo or later on, did you have any indication of how the Serbs reported alleged terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early days, there were situation maps produced through the Foreign Liaison Service, which was the service to which all defence attaches were accredited, which was a branch of the General Staff, and they attempted to portray every single instant that they thought was a terrorist action. I would suggest that this was a slightly a way of blowing up every incident into a major incident, rather than some of them which were some were clearly very minor incidents. But it was a question of numbers that were important rather than, you know, hard facts of what terrorists incidents were actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If the numbers were being -- actually, let me bring up Exhibit 938 at page 21, middle of the page. Sir, with regards to the way attacks are reported, terrorist attacks are reported by the Serbian side, did you find the numbers accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to that, again. The previous question was whether he was -- whether he knew how attacks were reported, then he said that defence liaison service would receive -- or was shown situation maps. That's the answer to the question. He has no way of evaluating numbers or as to whether they're accurate or inaccurate. There is no foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to establish a foundation, first of all, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You had indicated in one of your previous answers that the reporting was being blown up with regards to how they were qualifying what is a terrorist attack and what is not a terrorist attack. Can you expand on that answer a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's a factor of Serbian life that things are put down in -- in numerical order, and the higher the numbers the more important the case may be. And, as I said, I think this muddles the issue as to what were genuine terrorist incidents and worthy of report and what were just minor incursions or whatever, which just add to the general intelligence build-up. One needs to stick to -- to hard facts as to what was a terrorist incidents as opposed to what was reported to be a terrorist incident, which I think General Dimitrijevic is indicating in this particular statement,"that I commend that yesterday's two were conducted by us that we were not attacked, in other words we did not launch an operation following an attack on our unit by terrorists." So it's rather like claiming two points in tennis when you haven't actually played the ball.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before doing that, can you clarify for us the exhibits over which there may be remain a question mark? You have mentioned P1969 as one which you would seek to have admitted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's contained within the statement. He makes comment on it within the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we haven't actually seen the exhibit, have we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Based on the comments of the Court I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's an operational order?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour it's a Joint Command order, similar to the pun at P01968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there any other exhibits referred to in the statement which have not yet been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Which have not been exhibited, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the only own one, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P1990, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 14, I believe, Your Honour. The counsel said they are going to elicit some further factors, and I reserved my objections for the questions to be raised and no questions have been raised. So I would ask for that document -- for that portion of the statement then to be excluded, because again he's commenting about something and speculating about what a document might mean, and the document couldn't purport to reflect what his recollections are as set forth in paragraph 14. And we've heard nothing in his live testimony that would -- that would otherwise expand on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you challenging this document as -- as un-authentic?.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's already been admitted Your Honour, to another witness..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't see anything wrong with the statement there. The witness is saying what his experience is, and all he's saying is it's very similar to the one that Mr. O'Sullivan and indeed others objected to earlier. He's saying, well, that's consistent with what I actually saw, so that's quite different from what Vasiljevic was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But this document was shown to a witness who was actually present in the meeting, and that wasn't asked many him. So I find it very interesting how the Prosecution -- what picture they try to paint with documents and with witnesses who have a tangential relation to the documents, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's something we will hear in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree that's arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's really a matter of weight, and I take it there's no suggestion that there's anything wrong with 1969, which is the other one or the one that so far hasn't been admitted. Well, we shall note that there are no specific challenges. We haven't taken a decision on admitting the statement as yet, until we hear the rest of the evidence. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expected other colleagues to raise the same objection, but it is one of principle on part. First of all, in relation to this document, this witness cannot have a foundation in terms of authenticity, and he cannot give us any information with regard to a particular exhibit. So this is my objection in principle, and it has to do with P1969. And the same objection was made when Mr. Drewienkiewicz testified, and the Trial Chamber sustained that objection by Mr. Petrovic, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection to that document you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was the document that was shown to Mr. Drewienkiewicz, together with the 1967, 1968, and 1966, yes. And Mr. Petrovic pointed out the same thing. He said exactly what I repeated just now. And if I remember correctly, the Trial Chamber decided what it decided; that is to say, they refused to admit these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that P1969 is not an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither the witness nor I can judge whether it's an authentic document. It's not signed, so there is no signature. Since there is not a signature at the end of the document, we don't even know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're urging admission --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know who issued it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see that document, please, on the screen. 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I think I should point out when it came up the last time, we objected to it on behalf of General Pavkovic, and I believe the objection was sustained at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the Prosecution is re-urging the same arguments that have been made for the other documents that have been admitted. This was received pursuant to an RFA from the forces of the FRY and Serbia, that it by its nature that is an indicia of reliability, certainly as taken together with the other orders in the same series, that it has this -- within the four corners of it, they are quite similar, and that one has already been admitted which would lead that the other one is equally reliable. And we would just re-urge the arguments that we made with the submissions of the Prosecution on January 29th in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that issue tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the one last thing before we have to break, there is a report from UNDU regarding General Pavkovic that indicates that his medical situation may continue for a period of about three days. We're going to look into that immediately upon adjourning today and try to find out exactly what the situation is with him because I think he will not waive appearance during the cross-examination of this witness, and so we're hoping that he can recover and be here tomorrow and we'll find out as soon as we can and then let the Chamber know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you indicating the plan is actually to complete the cross-examination tomorrow all being well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only talking about my own cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will complete yours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It depends on my colleagues who are going ahead of me, Your Honour It may not complete tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that there is waiver in the knowledge that the illness might last three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there is a waiver for today only, Your Honour. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The doctor's comment is that it might last for three days, but I think the waiver is for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I would suggest you give thought to, Mr. Ackerman, is that there is no particular prejudice to Mr. Pavkovic having the cross-examination conducted in his absence, as long as a video is made available to him if he's fit to view it and the witness is not released until he's had the chance to review it and make sure that there is nothing he would have drawn your attention to or at least has an opportunity to draw your attention to anything he identifies by viewing it. Now, that depends on a measure of fitness. I appreciate that. But I ask you to give thought to that. It's a major problem in a case of this magnitude where there are so many accused that inevitably from time to time there will be a breakdown because of illness, and we have to be imaginative I think if we can in the circumstances to deal with it. But I appreciate that there could be a more serious situation which wouldn't allow us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you have -- you have hit the exact issue, and that is that -- that he would want to be able to communicate with me regarding matters during the examination that he thinks I should cross-examine about, and if it can be done by video and we can get there before the witness is released, I have no problem with doing it that way. I don't want to delay these proceedings unnecessarily in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to stop there for today, Mr. Crosland. Your evidence will continue tomorrow with cross-examination. You'll have been told this before, that overnight it is vital that you have no communication with anyone at all about your evidence. That's either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give. You can talk to anyone you like about any subject other than the evidence in this case. We'll go into closed session now so that you can leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Pavkovic not present in court]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.34 p.m.,
